Integration is normally incremental rather than all at once. Components are combined in a planned sequence, each addition tested before the next is made, so that when a fault appears the newly introduced element is the prime suspect. The alternative, assembling everything and then testing, produces a situation in which a fault could originate anywhere, and diagnosis becomes combinatorially difficult. Where a component is not yet available, a stub or simulator standing in for it allows integration to proceed, at the cost that the simulator embodies assumptions which may themselves be wrong.

Test facilities are a substantial engineering effort in their own right. Environmental testing subjects hardware to the temperature, vibration, shock, humidity, vacuum, radiation and electromagnetic conditions it will meet, usually with margin beyond the expected worst case. Qualification testing takes a dedicated unit beyond design limits to demonstrate margin exists, and often to destruction. Acceptance testing checks each delivered unit against its specification at less severe levels, since the purpose is to catch manufacturing defects rather than to re-prove the design.

Formal reviews punctuate the lifecycle and gate progress. The system requirements review confirms that requirements are complete and agreed. Preliminary design review confirms the architecture and allocation, typically with substantial margins still held. Critical design review confirms the detailed design is ready to build. Test readiness review confirms procedures, facilities and articles are prepared. Operational readiness review confirms the fielded system, its documentation, spares and trained personnel are ready for service. These reviews function well when they are genuine decision points with the authority to stop work, and poorly when they become presentations whose outcome was settled beforehand, which is a common and corrosive pattern.

Technology readiness levels, a nine-point scale originating at NASA in the 1970s and formalised in the 1990s, are used to judge whether the technologies a design depends on are mature enough to commit. Level one is basic principles observed; level six a prototype demonstrated in a relevant environment; level nine a system proven in operational use. The scale's practical value is as a warning: programmes that enter detailed design depending on technologies below roughly level six have historically suffered severe cost and schedule growth, because development risk and integration risk are then being carried simultaneously. The usual remedy is to run technology maturation as a separate activity, on its own schedule, with a fallback design that does not depend on it, so that the main programme is never held hostage to a research result.

sections.heading: Risk, Margin and Technical Budgets
sections.body:
Risk management is the systematic identification, assessment and treatment of things that might go wrong. Its object is not to eliminate risk, which is impossible, but to ensure that risks are known, owned, priced and watched rather than discovered late.

The conventional treatment characterises each risk by its likelihood and its consequence, often plotted on a matrix, and combines them into a rating that drives attention. Four responses are available: avoid, by changing the plan so the risk no longer applies; mitigate, by reducing likelihood or consequence; transfer, by insurance or contractual allocation, noting that transferring a risk to a supplier who cannot bear it merely disguises it; and accept, with the acceptance recorded and a contingency held. Every risk needs a named owner and a trigger condition specifying when a contingency plan will be invoked, because a plan with no trigger is not executed until it is too late.

The matrix has known weaknesses. Likelihood estimates for rare events are unreliable, categories such as high and medium are interpreted differently by different people, and the approach handles correlated risks poorly, treating as independent things that will in fact fail together. It is nonetheless useful as a communication device provided its limits are acknowledged.

Technical budgets are the systems engineer's most concrete tool for managing physical risk. A quantity such as mass, electrical power, memory, data bandwidth, thermal dissipation, cost or pointing error is allocated from the system level down to subsystems, and the sum of the allocations plus a held margin equals the system limit. Each subsystem is then accountable for staying within its allocation, and the current status of every budget is tracked continuously and reported at every review. When a subsystem needs more, the request comes to the system level, where it is granted from margin or traded against another subsystem, visibly.

Margin policy is deliberate rather than accidental. Spacecraft practice commonly holds mass margin of the order of thirty per cent at preliminary design review, reducing through the programme to a few per cent at launch as uncertainty resolves, and similar profiles apply to power and memory. Holding margin at the system level rather than distributing it into subsystem allocations is important, because margin hidden inside a subsystem is consumed silently by that subsystem and is unavailable when the system needs it.

The characteristic failure is margin erosion: a long series of individually small, individually justified increases that are each too minor to refuse and that collectively exhaust the reserve, leaving nothing when a genuine problem emerges late. The defence is to plot margin against time from the outset with a declared depletion profile, so that consumption faster than planned is visible as a trend at every review rather than as a crisis at the end. A margin chart that has been flat for six months and then falls off is telling a story that the individual change requests did not.

sections.heading: Specialty Disciplines: Reliability, Safety and Human Factors
sections.body:
Several specialist analyses run alongside mainstream design, and each contributes requirements that must be captured early because they are architectural.

Reliability engineering predicts and improves the probability that a system performs its function for a stated period under stated conditions. Its quantitative apparatus includes failure rates, mean time between failures, and reliability block diagrams that compute system reliability from component figures. Redundancy improves reliability at the cost of mass, power, complexity and new failure modes in the switching mechanism, and it is defeated entirely by common-cause failures, where one event disables all redundant paths at once: a single fire, a shared power supply, a common software fault, or identical design errors in identical units. Genuine independence is expensive and often only approximated.

Safety engineering asks how the system might cause harm and how that is prevented. Failure modes and effects analysis works bottom-up, considering each component's ways of failing and tracing the consequences, and is thorough but laborious and poor at catching combinations. Fault tree analysis works top-down from an undesired event, developed at Bell Laboratories in 1962 for the Minuteman missile programme, and handles combinations well. Hazard and operability studies, developed at Imperial Chemical Industries in the 1960s, walk a team through a design applying guide words such as no, more, less and reverse to each flow. Systems-theoretic process analysis, developed by Nancy Leveson, addresses a gap the others share: it treats accidents as arising from inadequate control rather than component failure, and therefore catches cases where every component worked as designed and the system still caused harm, which describes a large fraction of modern software-intensive accidents.

Human factors engineering treats the operator as part of the system rather than an inconvenience surrounding it. It addresses workload, situation awareness, display and control design, error tolerance, and the consequences of automation. A recurring and well-documented problem is the automation surprise, in which a system does something correct by its own logic that the operator did not expect and cannot readily diagnose, a pattern implicated in several aviation accidents. Designing so that failures are visible and recoverable matters more than designing so that they are rare.

Integrated logistics support addresses the fact that most of a long-lived system's cost is incurred after delivery. Maintainability, spares provisioning, diagnostics, documentation, training and disposal are engineered rather than assumed. A design that cannot be serviced without dismantling half the system will impose that cost for its entire life, and the decision that caused it will have been made in an afternoon.

Security engineering has joined this group as a first-class concern rather than an afterthought, for the same reason as safety: it is architectural. A system whose components trust one another implicitly cannot be secured by adding authentication later, and connectivity introduced for maintenance convenience has repeatedly become the route by which industrial and medical systems were compromised.

sections.heading: How It Fails, and What to Do About It
sections.body:
Large technical programmes fail in patterns regular enough to be catalogued, and the case histories are the discipline's most useful teaching material.

Requirements failures head the list. Specifications that are ambiguous, incomplete, or that capture a solution rather than a need produce systems built correctly to the wrong target. Interface failures follow, with the Mars Climate Orbiter's unit mismatch the standard illustration. Reuse without re-analysis is a distinct and dangerous category: Ariane 5 flight 501 was destroyed on 4 June 1996, about thirty-seven seconds after lift-off, because inertial reference software inherited from Ariane 4 converted a 64-bit floating-point horizontal velocity value into a 16-bit signed integer. Ariane 5's greater horizontal acceleration produced a value that overflowed, the software raised an unhandled exception, both redundant units failed identically because they ran the same code, and the vehicle broke up, destroying a payload and launcher worth some 370 million dollars. The offending calculation was not even needed after lift-off.

Organisational failures are at least as common as technical ones. The loss of Challenger on 28 January 1986 was proximately caused by an O-ring seal that lost resilience at low temperature, but the Rogers Commission found that engineers' concerns about cold-weather launch had been raised and overruled, and that the decision process had normalised a known anomaly over successive flights. Software-intensive safety failures show a similar shape: the Therac-25 radiation therapy machine caused six massive overdoses between 1985 and 1987, several fatal, through race conditions in control software combined with the removal of hardware interlocks that earlier models had, an inadequate error-reporting design and a manufacturer response that assumed the software could not be at fault.

The practical countermeasures follow directly. Invest in requirements and stakeholder understanding before design. Specify interfaces explicitly, including units, and check both sides. Re-verify reused components against the new environment rather than assuming inherited qualification carries over. Hold margin at system level and defend it. Make reviews genuine decision points with authority to stop. Ensure dissenting technical opinion has a route to decision-makers that does not pass through the person whose schedule it threatens. Track leading indicators such as requirements volatility, margin consumption and defect discovery rate, since these move before cost and schedule do.

Finally, keep the process proportionate. Systems engineering imposes real cost, and applying heavy formality to a small or exploratory project wastes effort and drives people to work around it. The question is always which of these activities the specific risk profile justifies, not how completely a standard can be complied with. Process applied without judgement produces documents rather than working systems, and the resulting paperwork can create a dangerous illusion that risks have been addressed simply because forms recording them have been completed and signed.

guides.title: Engineering project management
guides.summary: How engineering projects are planned, scheduled, costed, controlled and delivered: the constraint set, requirements, work breakdown, critical-path and earned-value methods, risk and change control, contracting and organisation, and the failure modes that sink real projects.

sections.heading: What engineering project management is, and why it is a distinct discipline
sections.body:
An engineering project is a temporary organisation assembled to create something that did not
exist before, under constraints of money, time and physical law, and then disbanded. That
definition carries more weight than it appears to. Because the organisation is temporary, it has
no accumulated habits to fall back on; because the product is new, no one has done exactly this
before; and because physical law is involved, some of the constraints are not negotiable no
matter how the schedule is drawn. Engineering project management is the discipline of getting
such an undertaking to a defined end state without running out of money, patience or time first.

It is worth separating it from operations management, which it superficially resembles.
Operations concerns repeated work: a plant producing the same casting a thousand times a week,
where the governing problem is variation around a known mean and the governing tools are
statistical process control and continuous improvement. Projects concern work done once, where
the governing problem is uncertainty about a mean nobody has measured yet. A technique that
works beautifully for reducing scrap on a production line, such as tightening tolerances by
studying historical output, has no historical output to study on a first-of-a-kind machine. This
is why importing manufacturing discipline wholesale into a research-heavy project usually
produces impressive documentation and a late delivery.

The discipline also differs from general management by the presence of technical truth. A
commercial manager can often negotiate a target; an engineering manager cannot negotiate the
speed of sound, the yield strength of a steel, or the settling time of a control loop. A large
part of the craft consists of knowing which numbers in a plan are commitments that people made
and which are consequences that nature imposes, and refusing to let the first category quietly
overwrite the second. When a schedule says concrete will be loaded at seven days, the twenty-
eight day design strength has not been reached and someone has made a technical decision by
scheduling accident.

The modern discipline dates roughly from the 1950s. The critical path method emerged from DuPont
in 1957 for plant shutdown planning, and the Program Evaluation and Review Technique from the
United States Navy's Polaris programme in 1958. Both were attempts to answer the same question:
in a network of thousands of interdependent activities, which ones actually determine the finish
date? Earned value grew from United States Air Force cost-control practice in the 1960s and was
codified as the Cost/Schedule Control Systems Criteria in 1967. Systems engineering, its close
sibling, formalised at Bell Labs and TRW over the same decades. The tools have been refined
since, but the underlying insight has not changed: on a project of any size, intuition about
progress is systematically wrong, and structured measurement is the only reliable correction.

sections.heading: The constraint set: beyond the iron triangle
sections.body:
Almost every introduction to the subject presents the iron triangle, in which scope, cost and
time form three sides of a figure and quality sits in the middle, with the claim that fixing any
two determines the third. As a first approximation this is useful and it survives because it is
true often enough to be worth saying. Its real value is rhetorical: it gives an engineer a
defensible way to answer a demand for more scope at constant cost and date, which is to ask
which of the other two the requester would like to move.

The model is nonetheless too simple for real work, in three specific ways. First, the trade is
not linear and it is not symmetric. Compressing a schedule buys time at a steeply rising
marginal cost, because the cheap accelerations, such as re-sequencing and overtime, are used
first, and the expensive ones, such as duplicating tooling or paying air freight on castings,
come later. A ten per cent schedule compression may cost five per cent more; a thirty per cent
compression may cost fifty per cent more and introduce defects that consume the saving. Second,
quality is not a free variable in the middle of the triangle. In safety-related work it is a
floor set by regulation and by professional duty, not a dial. A pressure vessel either meets its
code or it is not a pressure vessel.

Third, and least discussed, the triangle omits risk. Two plans with identical scope, cost and
duration can differ enormously in the probability that they will be achieved. A plan that
assumes a long-lead forging arrives on its first promised date and a plan that carries eight
weeks of float against that delivery look the same on a bar chart and are not the same
commitment. Mature practice therefore treats the constraint set as five-dimensional: scope,
cost, time, quality and risk, with resource availability sometimes separated out as a sixth
where skilled labour is genuinely scarce.

The practical use of this expanded set is in negotiation. When a sponsor asks for an earlier
date, the honest responses are enumerable: reduce scope, spend more, accept a lower probability
of success, or reduce quality where that is lawful and sensible. If none of those is permitted,
the date is not being negotiated, it is being wished for, and the project has just acquired its
first serious risk. Writing down which of the five is fixed, which is firm, and which is
flexible, at authorisation, is one of the highest-value hours available. Projects that never
held that conversation discover the answer later by collision, usually about two-thirds of the
way through, when all the flexibility has already been spent.

sections.heading: Life cycle, phases and the logic of stage gates
sections.body:
Engineering projects are conventionally divided into phases, and the division is not
bureaucratic decoration. It exists because the cost of changing a decision rises by roughly an
order of magnitude at each major transition, while the information available to make that
decision improves only gradually. Moving a wall on a drawing costs an hour. Moving it during
construction costs a week and a change order. Moving it after commissioning costs a shutdown.
The rational response is to spend disproportionate effort early, when changes are cheap, and to
protect the resulting decisions afterwards.

A typical sequence runs: concept, in which need is established and options are compared at low
fidelity; feasibility or front-end engineering, in which one option is developed far enough to
be costed with confidence; detailed design, in which the product is fully specified; procurement
and manufacture or construction; integration and test; commissioning and handover; operation;
and eventual decommissioning. Names vary by sector. Pharmaceutical development speaks of phases
I to III; software of discovery, delivery and support; civil engineering in the United Kingdom
uses the RIBA Plan of Work stages 0 to 7; the United States Department of Energy uses critical
decision points CD-0 through CD-4. The vocabulary is local, the logic is not.

Between phases sit gates. A gate is a scheduled decision point at which a defined body of
evidence is reviewed and one of four verdicts is issued: proceed, proceed with conditions, hold
pending specified work, or cancel. The fourth verdict is the one that gives the mechanism its
value, and it is the one most often quietly removed. A gate process in which cancellation has
never happened is not a control system, it is a ceremony, and everyone involved learns within
two cycles to prepare for it accordingly. Robert Cooper, who popularised the stage-gate model
for product development from the 1980s, was explicit that killing weak projects early is where
the return comes from, because it releases capacity for the strong ones.

The evidence a gate should demand is specific to the transition it guards. Before detailed
design, the useful question is whether the requirements are stable and the concept has been
shown to work in principle. Before manufacture, it is whether the design has been verified
against those requirements and whether the supply chain has been secured. Before commissioning,
it is whether test results demonstrate that the built article matches the design. Gates that ask
instead for a status presentation and a schedule reforecast collect no evidence and prevent
nothing.

Two failure patterns recur. Phase overlap, in which detailed design begins before the concept is
settled, is sometimes justified by schedule pressure and is sometimes simply avoidance of a
difficult decision; the cost surfaces later as rework. And gate inflation, in which the review
package grows until it takes three months to prepare, converts the control into the delay it was
meant to prevent. A gate package that cannot be assembled in a fortnight from work already
required for the engineering is asking for the wrong things.

sections.heading: Requirements: where most projects are decided
sections.body:
Study after study of failed engineering projects converges on the same root cause, and it is not
technical incompetence. It is requirements: absent, ambiguous, unstable, or agreed by people who
turned out not to have the authority to agree them. The reason is structural. Requirements are
written at the moment of least knowledge, in natural language, by parties with different
interests, and they are then treated as fixed truth by everyone downstream who never met the
author.

A requirement is a statement of what the delivered thing must do or must be, expressed so that
compliance can be judged without reference to the writer's intentions. That last clause carries
the work. The classic tests are that a good requirement is necessary, unambiguous, verifiable,
feasible, and free of design. "The pump shall be reliable" fails three of them. "The pump shall
achieve a mean time between failures of at least 20,000 hours when operated within the duty
envelope of Appendix B, demonstrated by accelerated life testing to the method of ISO 19973-2"
fails none. Verifiability is the sharpest filter available: if you cannot describe the test that
would settle an argument about compliance, you have written an aspiration.

Requirements are usefully separated into levels. Stakeholder or user requirements state the need
in the customer's language. System requirements restate that need as properties of the thing to
be built. Subsystem and component requirements allocate those properties downward. The chain
matters because it is what allows a change to be traced: if a customer relaxes a range
requirement, the allocation flowchart shows which battery, structure and thermal decisions can
now be revisited, and which cannot. A project without traceability answers that question by
convening a meeting and guessing.

The pathologies are recognisable. Gold-plating is the inclusion of requirements nobody asked for
because an engineer found them interesting; it is expensive and invisible, since no customer
will complain about extra capability at your cost. Implementation bias writes the solution into
the requirement, as in specifying a hydraulic actuator when the real need is a force and a
response time, which forecloses better options. Requirements creep is the steady accretion of
small additions each individually defensible; the honest defence is not to refuse changes but to
price every one, including its schedule effect, before accepting it. And the most damaging, the
unstated requirement, usually appears at acceptance testing in the form of a customer saying
that of course it needed to do that.

Practical countermeasures are unglamorous and effective. Number every requirement and never
reuse a number. Record for each one its source, its rationale, its verification method, and its
owner. Hold a formal baseline, after which changes go through change control rather than
conversation. And test the set for internal contradiction before it is issued, because a
specification that demands both minimum mass and a large safety factor on a fixed material has
already failed and only arithmetic will reveal it.

sections.heading: Work breakdown structure: decomposing the job
sections.body:
The work breakdown structure, or WBS, is a hierarchical decomposition of the total scope into
progressively smaller deliverables, ending in packages small enough to be estimated, assigned
and tracked. It is the least glamorous artefact in project management and arguably the most
load-bearing, because almost everything else, the schedule, the budget, the risk register, the
responsibility matrix and the reporting structure, is keyed to it. Two projects with equivalent
scope and different breakdowns will be managed very differently.

The essential discipline is that a WBS decomposes deliverables, not activities. The top level
names things: the airframe, the control system, the site works, the qualification test campaign.
Only at the lowest level does the decomposition turn into work packages that describe doing.
This ordering matters because deliverables are stable and activities are not; you can reorganise
how a wing is built ten times without changing the fact that a wing is required. A structure
built directly out of activities has to be rebuilt every time the method changes, taking the
cost baseline with it.

Two rules govern quality. The hundred per cent rule states that the children of any node sum to
exactly the parent, no more and no less: nothing in scope is missing, and nothing out of scope
has crept in. Its second half is regularly violated, most often by a helpful engineer adding a
deliverable the customer never bought. The mutual exclusivity rule states that no scope appears
in two branches, since duplicated scope is duplicated budget and, more dangerously, scope that
both owners believe the other is doing. Interfaces between branches are where this fails, which
is why mature structures include explicit integration work packages that own the seams.

How far to decompose is a judgement, and the useful heuristics are about control rather than
tidiness. A work package should be short enough that a status report between reviews is
meaningful, which in practice means its duration should not much exceed the reporting period; a
package of eighty hours to two weeks is a common target on construction, while a research task
may reasonably run longer with defined interim outputs. It should have one accountable owner, a
single cost account, a definable completion criterion that someone other than the doer can
check, and no internal dependency on another package's mid-point.

Each terminal package receives a WBS dictionary entry: a short statement of what is included,
what is explicitly excluded, the acceptance criterion, the owner and the estimating basis. The
exclusions line prevents more disputes than any other sentence in project documentation.
Finally, the WBS is crossed with the organisational breakdown structure to produce cost accounts
at the intersections, and with a responsibility assignment matrix, often in RACI form, so that
for every package exactly one name is accountable. Where two names appear, in practice none is.

sections.heading: Scheduling: networks, the critical path and float
sections.body:
A schedule is not a list of dates; it is a model of dependency from which dates are computed.
The central technique, the critical path method, represents each activity as a node with a
duration and draws arrows for logical dependencies, then performs two passes over the network.
The forward pass, working from the start, computes each activity's earliest start and earliest
finish. The backward pass, working from the required end, computes latest finish and latest
start. The difference between the early and late dates for an activity is its total float, the
amount it can slip without moving the project end. Activities with zero float form the critical
path, and the project's duration is the length of that path.

A small worked example fixes the idea. Suppose foundations take 10 days; steel erection takes 15
and needs foundations complete; cladding takes 12 and needs steel; the electrical rough-in takes
20 and also needs steel; and commissioning takes 5 and needs both cladding and electrical. The
steel branch to cladding gives 10 plus 15 plus 12, equalling 37 days before commissioning, while
the electrical branch gives 10 plus 15 plus 20, equalling 45. Commissioning cannot start until
day 45, so the project takes 50 days and the critical path runs foundations, steel, electrical,
commissioning. Cladding has 45 minus 37, or 8 days of float. That number is the most useful
output of the exercise, because it tells the manager exactly how much a cladding problem may
cost before it costs anything at all, and it warns that spending money to accelerate cladding
buys nothing.

Dependencies come in four logical types. Finish-to-start is the common case. Start-to-start with
a lag models overlapping work, such as beginning trenching two days after excavation starts.
Finish-to-finish ties completions, as when documentation must finish with the item it describes.
Start-to-finish is rare and usually indicates a modelling error. Lags should represent real
physical delay, such as concrete curing or paint drying, and should carry a note saying so; a
lag inserted to force a bar into a convenient place is a hidden assumption that will not update
when the network changes.

Two cautions matter more than the arithmetic. First, float belongs to the project, not to the
activity owner; if the cladding contractor absorbs all eight days as comfort, the project has
lost its buffer without anyone deciding to spend it. Second, the critical path is a property of
the current model, and it moves. As soon as electrical recovers four days, the two branches are
within four days of each other and cladding is nearly critical too. Near-critical paths,
conventionally those with float below about ten per cent of remaining duration, deserve almost
the same attention as the critical one, because on a real project several of them are usually
converging on the same resource.

sections.heading: Duration estimating, PERT and the arithmetic of uncertainty
sections.body:
Every activity duration in a schedule is a forecast, and forecasts made by the person who will
do the work carry a well-documented optimism. The bias is not dishonesty. It arises because
people estimate by imagining the job going as intended, and the intended path contains none of
the interruptions, rework, waiting for information and part-time attention that consume real
weeks. Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky named this the planning fallacy in 1979 and it has
survived every attempt to train it away, including in professionals estimating their own
repeated work.

The Program Evaluation and Review Technique, developed for the Polaris submarine programme in
1958, addressed the problem by asking for three numbers per activity instead of one: an
optimistic duration if everything goes well, a most likely duration, and a pessimistic duration
if the foreseeable things go wrong. The expected duration is then the weighted mean of the beta
distribution these imply, computed as optimistic plus four times most likely plus pessimistic,
all divided by six. The standard deviation is approximated as pessimistic minus optimistic
divided by six. If an activity is estimated at 8, 12 and 28 days, the expected duration is 8
plus 48 plus 28 over 6, which is 14 days, not the 12 that a single-point estimate would have
recorded, and the standard deviation is about 3.3 days.

The value of the three-point method is less in the formula than in the conversation. Asking what
the pessimistic case looks like forces an engineer to name the specific things that could go
wrong, which converts vague unease into a risk that can be managed. A twenty-day spread between
optimistic and pessimistic is a statement that the activity is poorly understood, and that is
worth knowing before it becomes the critical path.

Aggregation is where the arithmetic earns its keep and where it is most often misapplied.
Because independent variances add, the standard deviation of a path is the square root of the
sum of the activity variances, not their sum. Ten activities each with a 3.3-day standard
deviation give a path deviation of about 10.4 days, not 33. This is the mathematical case
against padding every activity: protection added at the activity level is far larger than the
protection the path actually needs, and it is invisible, so it gets consumed by Parkinson's law
and the student syndrome, in which work expands to fill the time and starts at the last
plausible moment. Consolidating the padding into a single visible project buffer, the core
insight of Eliyahu Goldratt's critical chain method from 1997, protects the same finish date
with less total time and makes buffer consumption a measurable early warning.

The honest caveat is that PERT's independence assumption is usually false. A labour shortage or
a design error affects many activities at once, and correlated variance does add nearly
linearly. PERT therefore systematically understates schedule risk on real projects, which is why
quantitative schedule risk analysis by Monte Carlo simulation, with correlation deliberately
modelled, has largely replaced the closed-form calculation on major work.

sections.heading: Resources, levelling, and why adding people can slow a project
sections.body:
A network schedule computed from logic alone assumes that whatever an activity needs will be
available when it starts. That assumption fails as soon as two parallel activities want the same
welder, the same test chamber or the same senior control engineer. Resource-constrained
scheduling resolves the conflict, and it always costs something: either the finish date moves,
or the resource level moves, and there is no third option.

The two standard treatments are distinguished by which variable is protected. Resource levelling
holds the resource limit fixed and lets the end date slip, delaying activities within and then
beyond their float until demand fits capacity; it is what you do when the constraint is real,
such as a single vacuum chamber. Resource smoothing holds the end date fixed and uses only
available float to flatten the demand profile, which reduces peaks without extending the project
but cannot help once float is exhausted. Levelling is a genuinely hard combinatorial problem, so
commercial tools use heuristics, typically prioritising activities with least float first. The
result is a valid schedule but rarely the optimal one, and the priority rule chosen can change
the computed finish by weeks, which is worth knowing before quoting the output as a fact.

The deeper point concerns adding people. Fred Brooks, from his experience managing the IBM
OS/360 development, formulated in 1975 what is now called Brooks's law: adding manpower to a
late software project makes it later. The mechanism is specific and generalises well beyond
software. New staff are unproductive for a ramp-up period and consume the time of the
experienced staff who must train them, so short-term output falls before it rises. And
communication overhead grows with the square of team size, because the number of pairwise
channels among n people is n times n minus one, over two. Going from 5 to 10 people doubles the
headcount but takes potential channels from 10 to 45.

Consequently the effect of extra staff depends on whether the remaining work is partitionable.
Pouring a larger concrete slab absorbs more labour almost linearly. Debugging a single subtle
control instability does not, and putting three more engineers on it mainly generates meetings.
A useful test before authorising an increase is to ask what specific separable deliverable each
new person will own, with what interface to the existing work; if the answer is that they will
help, the addition will probably hurt.

Two further realities deserve statement. Sustained overtime buys output for perhaps two to four
weeks and then gives it back through error rates and turnover, an effect measured repeatedly in
construction productivity studies. And multitasking across projects is not free: each switch
costs re-orientation, so an engineer split across three projects delivers materially less than
three one-third engineers and finishes everything later than sequential attention would have.

sections.heading: Cost estimating, contingency and reference-class forecasting
sections.body:
Cost estimates are produced at every phase, and their accuracy is bounded by what is known, not
by the effort spent computing them. The Association for the Advancement of Cost Engineering
International publishes a five-class scheme that makes this explicit. A Class 5 estimate, made
at zero to two per cent project definition, carries a typical range of minus 20 to plus 50 per
cent or worse. A Class 3, at ten to forty per cent definition, might run minus 10 to plus 30. A
Class 1, built from near-complete detailed design, might achieve minus 3 to plus 15. The
narrowing is called the cone of uncertainty, and the important consequence is that a precise-
sounding number quoted early is not more accurate for being precise; quoting 14.7 million at
concept stage communicates a confidence the method cannot support.

Methods scale with definition. Analogous estimating scales a known past project by size or
capacity, often using a power law such as the six-tenths rule for process plant, in which cost
ratio equals capacity ratio raised to about 0.6, so doubling throughput costs roughly 1.52 times
as much rather than twice. Parametric estimating fits a statistical model to historical data, as
in cost per square metre of a building type or per kilogram of spacecraft dry mass. Bottom-up
estimating sums resource requirements per work package and is the most accurate and the most
expensive, requiring a mature WBS. Serious estimates are usually built one way and checked
another, because the two methods fail differently and agreement is evidence.

Contingency is money set aside for things that will happen but cannot yet be named individually:
the statistical residue of small unknowns and identified risks. It is not padding, and its size
should be derived rather than picked; a flat ten per cent is a confession that no analysis was
done. Where risk has been quantified, contingency is set at a chosen confidence level from the
risk model, commonly the eightieth percentile, so that the budget has an eighty per cent chance
of sufficing. Separate from contingency is management reserve, held above the baseline by the
sponsor for genuinely unforeseen scope, and controlled by them rather than by the project
manager.

The most consequential finding in the field belongs to Bent Flyvbjerg, whose studies of hundreds
of large infrastructure projects from the 1990s onward found systematic, non-random cost
overruns: rail averaging around 45 per cent, bridges and tunnels around 34 per cent, roads
around 20 per cent, with no improvement over seventy years. He attributes this to optimism bias
plus strategic misrepresentation, that is, estimates shaped by the need to win approval. His
proposed corrective, reference-class forecasting, ignores the inside view of your own plan and
instead takes the distribution of outcomes from a class of similar completed projects, then
places your project within it. The method is uncomfortable precisely because it overrides
detailed reasoning with base rates, and the evidence is that the base rates usually win.

sections.heading: Earned value: measuring progress in money
sections.body:
The oldest question in project control is whether a project reporting sixty per cent of its
budget spent is ahead, behind or on plan. Spend alone cannot answer it, and neither can a
percentage complete asserted by the people doing the work. Earned value management answers it by
measuring three quantities in the same units, normally money or labour hours, and comparing
them.

Planned value is the budgeted cost of the work scheduled to be complete by the reporting date.
Actual cost is what has been spent on the work performed. Earned value, the invention that makes
the system work, is the budgeted cost of the work actually performed, calculated by taking the
original budget for each completed or partly completed package and crediting it according to
physical progress. Because earned value and planned value are both expressed in budget terms,
their difference isolates schedule performance; because earned value and actual cost both refer
to the same completed work, their difference isolates cost performance.

A worked example. A project has a 1,000,000 unit budget over ten months, spending evenly. At the
end of month four, planned value is 400,000. Physical progress assessed against the WBS shows
work worth 340,000 of original budget completed, so earned value is 340,000. Invoices total
400,000, so actual cost is 400,000. The schedule variance is earned value minus planned value,
or minus 60,000, and the schedule performance index is 340,000 over 400,000, which is 0.85: the
project is achieving 85 per cent of the planned rate. The cost variance is earned value minus
actual cost, minus 60,000, and the cost performance index is 340,000 over 400,000, again 0.85:
every unit spent is buying 0.85 units of budgeted work. The naive reading, that spend equals
plan and all is well, was wrong on both axes.

Forecasting follows directly. If the cost performance index observed to date is assumed to
persist, the estimate at completion is the budget at completion divided by that index, here
1,000,000 over 0.85, or about 1,176,000, implying an overrun near 176,000. The empirical
justification is substantial: research on United States defence programmes, notably by David
Christensen in the 1990s, found that once a project is around twenty per cent complete, the
cumulative cost performance index rarely improves by more than about ten per cent and typically
worsens. The instinct to promise recovery in the second half is, statistically, almost always
wrong.

Two warnings. The schedule index is denominated in money, not time, and it converges to 1.0 at
completion even on a project finishing a year late, because eventually all planned value is
earned; past about the two-thirds point it must be read alongside the critical path or replaced
by earned schedule, a refinement introduced by Walt Lipke in 2003 that converts earned value
back into time. And the whole system is only as honest as the progress measurement beneath it,
which is why rules such as 0/100 credit, where a package earns nothing until finished, or 50/50
credit at start and finish, are preferred to an engineer's judgement of being nearly there.

sections.heading: Risk management: identification, analysis and response
sections.body:
Risk in project work means an uncertain event or condition which, if it occurs, changes an
objective. The definition deliberately includes upside, since an opportunity ignored is as much
a management failure as a threat unmanaged, though in practice threat handling dominates. The
discipline exists because the alternative, dealing with problems as they arrive, forfeits the
cheapest interventions: almost every risk is cheaper to prevent or prepare for than to absorb.

Identification is the step most often done badly, because it is done once, in a workshop, by the
people already committed to the plan. Better practice draws on several independent sources: a
prompt list or risk breakdown structure covering technical, external, organisational and
management categories; the lessons register from comparable past projects; assumption analysis,
in which every assumption in the plan is restated as the risk that it is wrong; and a pre-
mortem, Gary Klein's 2007 technique in which the team is told to imagine the project has failed
catastrophically and to write the history. The pre-mortem works because prospective hindsight
loosens the social constraint against predicting failure in front of the sponsor.

Qualitative analysis scores each risk for probability and impact, usually on ordinal scales, and
plots them on a matrix to set priority. It is fast and adequate for most items, but it has two
known pathologies. Ordinal scores are not numbers and multiplying them is arithmetic without
meaning, so a "high times low" cell can conceal a rare event that would end the project. And
risk matrices compress distinct situations into the same cell, so a frequent small nuisance and
a rare disaster can score alike. Any risk capable of causing project failure should therefore be
escalated regardless of its computed score.

Quantitative analysis models the aggregate. Monte Carlo simulation samples each uncertain
duration or cost from its distribution thousands of times and produces a distribution of
outcomes, from which a confidence level can be read: the date with an eighty per cent chance of
being met, for instance. Its outputs are only as good as its inputs, and the most common error
is treating variables as independent when a single cause drives many, which understates the
tails. Sensitivity analysis, often displayed as a tornado diagram, is frequently the more
valuable output, since it names the few variables that actually drive the spread.

Responses fall into a small set. Avoid, by changing the plan so the risk cannot arise, such as
choosing a proven component over a novel one. Transfer, by contract or insurance, remembering
that transfer moves consequence rather than removing it and that a bankrupt supplier transfers
it back. Mitigate, by reducing probability or impact, which is where most engineering effort
goes: qualifying a second source, building a prototype, adding schedule float ahead of a known
cliff. Or accept, either actively with a funded contingency plan and a named trigger, or
passively. Every entry should carry an owner, a date and a trigger condition, because a risk
register reviewed monthly and never acted upon is a document, not a control.

sections.heading: Change control, configuration management and interfaces
sections.body:
Once a baseline exists, the project's central administrative problem is knowing what the current
definition of the product is and ensuring everyone is working to it. Configuration management is
the discipline that answers this, and its absence produces a characteristic failure: two parts
machined from different revisions of the same drawing that do not fit, discovered at assembly,
months after the money was spent.

The discipline has four classical elements. Configuration identification selects the items to be
controlled and gives each a unique identifier and revision. Configuration control governs how
changes to those items are proposed, evaluated and approved. Status accounting records what the
current approved configuration is, and what each delivered unit was built to. Configuration
audit verifies that the physical article matches the documentation, which is the step that
catches undocumented workshop fixes before they become a maintenance mystery a decade later.

Change control is the human machinery around this. A change request should state what is to
change, why, and its assessed effect on cost, schedule, risk, performance, safety and any
regulatory approval already granted. That assessment is engineering work and takes time; a
change board that approves proposals on the strength of a verbal estimate is deciding without
information. Approval authority is usually tiered by significance, with minor changes delegated
to a project-level board and changes touching customer-visible requirements, safety cases or
contract value escalated. The most valuable habit is to record rejected changes with reasons,
because the same idea returns every six months until its refusal is documented.

Interfaces deserve separate treatment because they are where projects break. An interface is a
boundary across which two parties must agree, and the defining hazard is that each side
reasonably believes the other is handling the ambiguity. Formal practice maintains an interface
register, and for anything significant an interface control document that specifies the boundary
in verifiable terms: mechanical envelope and mounting, mass and centre of gravity, electrical
connector type, pinout, voltage and current limits, data protocol and rates, thermal loads to be
rejected, and the timing of who provides what to whom. Each interface has two named owners, one
per side, and a scheduled agreement date, because an interface agreed late has already caused
rework on both sides.

The economic argument for all this rigour is asymmetric. Configuration management is a steady,
visible overhead of a few per cent, and its failures are rare, large and often unattributable to
the missing process. That asymmetry is why it is cut first under schedule pressure and why the
cut is usually a mistake. The Mars Climate Orbiter, lost in September 1999 because one team
supplied impulse data in pound-force seconds while the receiving software expected newton-
seconds, is the canonical illustration: not an engineering error in either team's own frame, but
an interface that nobody owned.

sections.heading: Procurement, contracts and the incentives they create
sections.body:
On most engineering projects the majority of the value is bought rather than made in-house, so
the contract is not a legal afterthought; it is the control system for most of the budget. The
key insight is that a contract type distributes risk, and whoever holds a risk will price it,
manage it or be destroyed by it. Choosing a type is therefore an engineering decision about
which party is better placed to control the uncertainty.

Firm fixed price fixes the payment regardless of the supplier's cost. It suits well-defined
scope, transfers cost risk to the supplier, and buys the client administrative simplicity. Its
hidden mechanics are that the supplier prices the risk into the bid, often generously, and that
once margin is threatened the supplier's rational behaviour is to minimise anything not
explicitly required and to pursue variations aggressively. A fixed price on an ill-defined scope
does not eliminate the client's exposure; it converts it into claims.

Cost reimbursable contracts pay recorded cost plus a fee, keeping cost risk with the client.
They suit genuinely uncertain work such as first-of-a-kind development or emergency repair,
where a supplier cannot price the unknown without an unaffordable premium. The weakness is the
incentive: cost plus a percentage fee rewards spending, which is why that variant is prohibited
in United States federal procurement. Cost plus fixed fee is neutral on spending. Cost plus
incentive fee shares under-run and over-run according to a stated ratio, for example 80:20, up
to a ceiling; the share line, not the fee, is what actually shapes behaviour.

Target cost contracts, common in United Kingdom infrastructure under the NEC suite, set a target
and share the difference between target and outturn under a pain and gain formula. Their intent
is to align the parties, and they work when the target is realistic and the cost records are
open. When the target is set optimistically to win approval, the mechanism converts into an
argument about compensation events roughly two-thirds of the way through the job.

Beyond type, several clauses do disproportionate work. The definition of scope, usually by
reference to a specification and drawing list at stated revisions, determines what counts as a
variation. Liquidated damages set an agreed sum per day of delay, which caps the supplier's
exposure as much as it protects the client, and which is unenforceable if it is a penalty rather
than a genuine estimate of loss. Retention and milestone payment schedules control cash and
therefore attention. Warranty and defects liability periods govern who pays for problems that
appear in service. And the change mechanism, including how many days the supplier has to notify
a claim, decides most disputes years later. Practically, the client's obligations are the ones
most often missed: late free-issue material or late approval of a drawing is a client-caused
delay, and a competent supplier will be recording it from the first week even if it is never
mentioned in a progress meeting.

sections.heading: Organising the work: team structures and delivery methods
sections.body:
Where a project sits in an organisation determines how much authority its manager actually has,
and authority mismatched to accountability is one of the most reliable predictors of trouble.
Three classical arrangements exist. In a functional organisation, staff belong to departments
and the project coordinator has little formal power; work is done through negotiation with
department heads and priorities are set by them, which suits small projects inside a stable
operating business. In a projectised organisation, staff are assigned wholly to the project
under a manager with full authority, which suits large, long, autonomous work but strands people
when the project ends. The matrix sits between, with staff reporting both to a functional home
and to a project, and it is described as weak, balanced or strong according to where the power
sits. The matrix is the common arrangement and the least comfortable one, since it
institutionalises competing claims on the same person. It works only when escalation is fast and
someone is empowered to settle contention within days rather than weeks.

Delivery method is a separate axis, and the correct choice follows from the shape of the
uncertainty rather than from fashion. Predictive or plan-driven delivery, in which requirements
are baselined and then executed, is appropriate when requirements can be known in advance and
the cost of change is high: a bridge, a pressure system, a certified aircraft component. Its
strength is that it permits efficient procurement and construction sequencing; its weakness is
brittleness when the requirement was wrong.

Iterative and incremental methods, of which the agile family formalised by the 2001 Agile
Manifesto is the best known, accept that requirements will be learned and structure the work as
repeated short cycles, each producing something inspectable. This is powerful where change is
cheap and feedback is informative, which is why it dominates software. Applying it wholesale to
physical projects fails on the economics: you cannot iterate a poured foundation in two-week
sprints. What does transfer is the principle beneath it, which is to shorten the feedback loop
on whatever is genuinely uncertain, and that is achieved in hardware through prototypes, test
rigs, mock-ups and simulation rather than through sprints of construction.

Most substantial engineering programmes therefore end up hybrid, and deliberately so: agile or
spiral development for software and control logic, set-based concurrent engineering for early
design options, and a predictive, gated backbone for procurement, manufacture and commissioning
where commitments are irreversible. Lean thinking contributes a third strand, focused on flow
and the elimination of waiting; the Last Planner System in construction, developed by Glenn
Ballard and Greg Howell in the 1990s, improves reliability by having the people who will do next
week's work commit to it only after confirming its prerequisites are ready. The organising
question in all cases is where the expensive irreversibility lies, and that is where planning
discipline belongs.

sections.heading: Verification, validation, commissioning and handover
sections.body:
Two distinct questions must be answered before a project can be considered finished, and
confusing them is a classic and expensive error. Verification asks whether the thing was built
to the specification, that is, whether it meets the requirements as written. Validation asks
whether it meets the actual need, that is, whether the requirements were right. Barry Boehm's
1979 phrasing remains the clearest: verification is building the product right, validation is
building the right product. A system can pass every verification test and be useless, which is
what happens when a requirement was misinterpreted at the outset, and this is precisely why the
customer must be involved in validation rather than only in acceptance.

Verification uses four recognised methods, chosen per requirement and recorded in the
verification matrix. Inspection confirms by examination, appropriate for markings, materials and
workmanship. Analysis confirms by calculation or simulation, used where a test is impossible or
destructive, such as fatigue life over thirty years. Demonstration confirms that a function
operates, without necessarily measuring a quantity. Test confirms by measurement against stated
tolerances under controlled conditions, and is the strongest evidence. Every requirement should
be traceable to at least one method and to the evidence produced, which is what makes an
acceptance argument auditable rather than a matter of confidence.

Commissioning is the process of bringing a completed installation into operation, and on process
plant and buildings it is where the schedule most often overruns, because it is planned last and
depends on everything else being finished. It proceeds in an order that reflects risk:
mechanical completion, confirming that construction matches the drawings and that systems are
clean, aligned and supported; pre-commissioning checks such as pressure testing, loop checks and
instrument calibration; energisation and cold commissioning without process fluid or load; then
hot commissioning with real material, followed by performance testing against guaranteed
figures. Each step is deliberately system-based rather than area-based, which is why
commissioning engineers should influence the construction sequence months earlier; a contractor
optimising for construction efficiency will finish areas, and commissioning cannot start on a
partial system.

Handover transfers custody, and the mistake is to treat it as an event rather than a package.
What the operator needs includes as-built drawings reflecting site changes, operating and
maintenance manuals, spares lists with lead times, calibration and test certificates, statutory
approvals, training delivered to named people, and the defects list with owners and dates. A
punch list closed by the contractor's own signature is worth little; an operator who accepts a
system without a maintenance plan will be running it on heroics within a year. Finally, closeout
should include a documented lessons review conducted honestly and early enough that the team
still remembers, together with formal release of staff and closure of contracts and accounts,
because projects left administratively open continue to accrue cost for years.

sections.heading: How projects fail, and how to recover one
sections.body:
Failure in engineering projects is rarely a single dramatic event. The characteristic pattern is
a slow accumulation of small, individually reasonable decisions, each taken under pressure,
whose combined effect only becomes visible when the remaining float has gone. Recognising the
pattern early is worth more than any recovery technique, because the options available shrink
continuously.

The recurring root causes are a short list. Requirements that were never stable, so design work
is repeatedly invalidated. A schedule that was never achievable, adopted because it was required
rather than because it was computed. Underestimated integration, where every component works and
the assembled system does not, which is the standard fate of projects that planned integration
as a short activity at the end. Optimistic reporting, in which status is expressed as a
percentage that nobody can audit and problems are held at the level where they arose in the hope
of local recovery. Key-person dependency, discovered when that person resigns. Interface
ownership gaps. And scope growth accepted without corresponding time or money, which is the
polite form of all the others.

Early indicators are more reliable than they are comfortable. A cost performance index below 0.9
at twenty per cent complete has strong historical predictive power for overrun. Float erosion on
the critical path over consecutive reporting periods, rather than absolute lateness, is the
earliest schedule signal. A rising count of open actions, unanswered technical queries or
unresolved non-conformances indicates a system taking on debt. Repeated re-baselining is
diagnostic on its own, since each re-baseline resets the variance measurements that would
otherwise reveal the trend. And a qualitative signal that experienced managers trust: when
reporting becomes noticeably more optimistic than corridor conversation, the formal system has
stopped carrying information.

Recovery begins with an honest reassessment, which usually requires someone with no ownership of
the original plan, because the team cannot easily abandon a position it has defended for a year.
The sequence that works is to stop and establish ground truth by re-measuring physical
completion rather than accepting reported percentages; to rebuild the remaining schedule bottom-
up from where things actually are, not by compressing the old plan; to renegotiate the
constraint set explicitly with the sponsor, since a recovery plan that assumes the original
scope, cost and date is a second work of fiction; to reduce work in progress and concentrate
resources on finishing rather than starting; and to attack the integration and test path first,
because that is where the unknowns concentrate.

The hardest decision is cancellation, and it is made badly for a known reason: sunk cost. Money
already spent is irrelevant to whether the remaining spend is worthwhile, yet it dominates the
discussion. The correct question is whether the value of completion exceeds the cost still to
come, answered with the estimate you now believe rather than the one you approved. Projects
cancelled at forty per cent complete are often described as failures, but a project that spends
its full budget delivering something the organisation no longer needs has failed considerably
more expensively.

guides.title: Engineering economics and cost estimating
guides.summary: How engineers compare designs and projects in money terms: the time value of money, present worth, rate of return, depreciation and taxes, replacement decisions, and the craft of building and defending cost estimates.

sections.heading: Why every engineering decision is an economic decision
sections.body: In 1887 the American railway engineer Arthur Mellen Wellington opened his book The Economic Theory of the Location of Railways with a definition that has never been improved on: engineering, he wrote, is the art of doing well with one dollar what any bungler can do with two after a fashion. The remark captures something that separates engineering from pure science. A physicist asks whether a thing can be done; an engineer must also ask whether it is worth doing, and worth doing this way rather than some other way. Nearly every technical choice is at bottom a choice among competing uses of limited money, labor, energy, and time. Should a bridge be steel or prestressed concrete? Should a factory buy the efficient pump that costs three times as much? Should a worn machine be overhauled again or replaced? Should a road be built at all? None of these questions can be answered by stress calculations alone, because the alternatives all work. They differ in what they cost, when those costs arrive, what they earn or save, and how long they last, and the discipline that compares alternatives on exactly those terms is engineering economics. Its companion craft, cost estimating, answers the prior question: what will this thing actually cost to build and to own? An analysis is only as good as the numbers fed into it, and producing credible numbers for something that does not yet exist is a demanding skill with its own methods, standards, and famous failure modes. Together the two subjects form the money side of engineering practice. They are tested on the Fundamentals of Engineering examination, embedded in every corporate capital-approval process, and written into law for public works in many countries. The core intellectual move of the whole field is a single idea: money has a time value, so cash flows occurring at different dates cannot be added or compared directly. A dollar today is worth more than a dollar next year, because today's dollar can be invested to become more than a dollar by next year, and because a promise of future money carries risk and is eroded by inflation. Once cash flows are translated to a common point in time using an interest rate, alternatives with wildly different shapes, such as cheap-to-build but expensive-to-run versus the reverse, become directly comparable. Around that one move the field builds a toolkit: equivalence factors that shift money through time, decision criteria such as present worth and rate of return, adjustments for taxes, depreciation, and inflation, and methods for handling uncertainty. This guide develops the toolkit from first principles, works numerical examples, then turns to cost estimating: how estimates are classified by maturity, how parametric shortcuts like the six-tenths rule and cost indices work, why learning curves lower unit costs, and why large-project estimates fail so often and so predictably. A reader who absorbs it should be able to set up a comparison correctly, compute it, and defend the numbers behind it.

sections.heading: Cash flows, interest, and the time value of money
sections.body: The raw material of every analysis is the cash flow: a movement of money in or out at a stated time. Engineering economics deliberately ignores accounting abstractions and tracks only actual money crossing the boundary of the project or firm, receipts counted positive and disbursements negative. The universal bookkeeping device is the cash flow diagram, a horizontal time axis marked off in periods, usually years, with upward arrows for income and downward arrows for costs. By convention, time zero is the present, a first cost is drawn at time zero, and recurring amounts such as maintenance are drawn at the end of the period in which they accrue; this end-of-period convention is arbitrary but must be applied consistently, because the standard formulas assume it. Drawing the diagram before computing anything is not a beginner's crutch. It is how experienced analysts catch the misplaced overhaul, the forgotten salvage value, or the rent that starts in year three rather than year one. Interest is the price paid for the use of money over time, exactly as rent is the price paid for the use of a building. If a bank lends 10,000 dollars for a year and receives 10,800 back, the interest is 800 dollars and the interest rate is 8 percent per year. From the lender's side, interest is compensation for three distinct things: the postponement of consumption, the risk that the borrower defaults, and the expected erosion of purchasing power by inflation. That is why rates differ across borrowers and across eras, and why a government bond yields less than a loan to a startup. For decision-making inside a firm, the rate that matters is the minimum attractive rate of return, abbreviated MARR: the return the organization insists on before it will tie up capital in a project. The MARR is a policy number, not a market observation. It is typically set at or above the firm's cost of capital, the blended cost of its debt and equity financing, and is often raised for riskier ventures; a utility might use 8 percent while a technology company demands 25. Every do-nothing alternative implicitly earns the MARR, because money not spent on the project is presumed invested elsewhere at that rate. This is the concept of opportunity cost, and it explains a rule that surprises newcomers: an alternative can be profitable in the everyday sense and still be rejected, because accepting it would forgo something better. The entire apparatus that follows, equivalence factors, present worth, rate of return, is machinery for answering one question: given the timing of these cash flows and given this MARR, which alternative leaves the organization wealthiest? Keeping that question in view prevents the most common conceptual error, which is treating the mathematics as an end in itself rather than as a comparison of real alternatives that must be defined honestly, including the alternative of doing nothing at all.

sections.heading: Simple interest, compound interest, and the Rule of 72
sections.body: There are two ways to charge interest, and the difference between them compounds, literally, into enormous sums. Under simple interest, the charge is computed only on the original principal. Lend P at rate i per year for n years and the borrower repays F equal to P multiplied by the quantity one plus n times i; at 8 percent, 10,000 dollars grows to 18,000 in ten years. Under compound interest, each period's interest is added to the principal and itself earns interest thereafter, so the balance after n periods is P multiplied by the quantity one plus i raised to the power n. The same loan compounds to 10,000 times 1.08 to the tenth power, which is 21,589 dollars, a fifth more than the simple case, and the gap widens without limit as time runs on. Compound interest is the norm in virtually all commerce and is assumed everywhere in engineering economics; simple interest survives mainly in short-term notes and some legal judgments. The practice is ancient. Clay tablets show Babylonian scribes computing compound growth on loans of silver and barley nearly four thousand years ago, and one Old Babylonian exercise asks how long silver takes to double at the standard 20 percent, an early version of a question every analyst still asks. The modern shortcut for that question is the Rule of 72: at i percent per period, a sum doubles in approximately 72 divided by i periods. Money at 6 percent doubles in about twelve years, at 9 percent in about eight, at 12 percent in about six. The rule follows from the mathematics of logarithms, since exact doubling time is the natural log of 2, about 0.693, divided by the natural log of one plus i, and 72 is used instead of 69 because it divides evenly by so many small numbers; the approximation is excellent for rates between roughly 4 and 15 percent. The rule provides a fast sanity check that catches gross errors before they propagate. If a spreadsheet claims that 1 million dollars invested at 7 percent becomes 16 million in twenty years, the rule says doubling takes about ten years, so twenty years gives two doublings and roughly 4 million; the spreadsheet is wrong by a factor of four. The exponential character of compounding also explains why the interest rate dominates every long-lived analysis. Over a 40-year facility life, a difference between discounting at 3 percent and at 7 percent changes the present value of a distant dollar by a factor of more than four, which is why the choice of rate in public-sector studies, discussed later in this guide, is fought over so fiercely. It also explains why small recurring costs deserve respect: a 1,000 dollar annual maintenance saving, compounded at 8 percent over 30 years, accumulates to more than 113,000 dollars of future value. Intuition tuned to straight lines consistently underestimates exponential growth, and much of learning this subject is retraining that intuition with the formulas.

sections.heading: The six equivalence factors and a worked loan example
sections.body: Equivalence is the load-bearing concept of the field: two cash flow patterns are equivalent at interest rate i if they can be exchanged for one another without changing anyone's wealth. Six standard factors convert among the three basic patterns, a single present amount P, a single future amount F, and a uniform end-of-period series A. Each factor is written with a mnemonic slash notation naming what you want and what you have. The single-payment compound amount factor, F given P, equals one plus i raised to the n; its reciprocal, P given F, discounts a future sum to the present. The uniform-series compound amount factor, F given A, equals the quantity one plus i to the n minus one, all divided by i, and turns level deposits into a future balance; its reciprocal, A given F, is called the sinking fund factor because nineteenth-century companies used it to size the annual deposit that would sink, or retire, a bond issue at maturity. The series present worth factor, P given A, equals the quantity one plus i to the n minus one, divided by i times one plus i to the n; its reciprocal, A given P, is the capital recovery factor, the most used formula in the subject, because it answers the question every owner asks: what level annual amount does this purchase really cost me over its life? A worked example makes the machinery concrete. Consider a 200,000 dollar mortgage at a 6 percent nominal annual rate with monthly compounding over 30 years. The period is the month, so i is 0.005 and n is 360. The capital recovery factor is 0.005 times 1.005 to the 360th power, divided by 1.005 to the 360th minus one. Since 1.005 to the 360th is about 6.0226, the factor is 0.030113 divided by 5.0226, or 0.0059955, and the payment is about 1,199 dollars per month. Total payments come to roughly 431,700 dollars, so interest exceeds the principal itself, a fact the factor makes visible at a glance. The same factor sizes the annual cost of a 50,000 dollar machine over ten years at 12 percent: multiply by 0.1770 to get 8,850 dollars per year. Two further factors handle cash flows that grow. The arithmetic gradient factors convert a series rising by a constant amount G each period, such as maintenance that climbs 500 dollars per year as equipment ages, into an equivalent uniform series or present worth. The geometric gradient present worth factor handles series growing at a constant percentage, the natural model for costs that track inflation. Before electronic calculators, every textbook carried pages of factor tables at standard rates, and the notation was designed for looking things up; today a spreadsheet computes the formulas directly, but the notation survives because it forces the analyst to state what is known, what is sought, the rate, and the number of periods, which is precisely the discipline that prevents most setup errors.

sections.heading: Nominal and effective rates, continuous compounding, and inflation
sections.body: Interest rates are quoted in ways designed, sometimes deliberately, to confuse, and the analyst must translate every quote into a consistent form before computing. A nominal rate, called the annual percentage rate or APR in consumer lending, is a period rate multiplied by the number of periods per year, with compounding ignored. A credit card quoting 18 percent APR compounded monthly actually charges 1.5 percent each month, and because each month's interest itself earns interest, the effective annual rate is 1.015 raised to the twelfth power minus one, which is 19.56 percent. The general relation is that the effective rate equals one plus r over m, raised to the m, minus one, where r is the nominal rate and m the number of compounding periods per year. The gap between nominal and effective widens with the frequency of compounding: 18 percent nominal is 19.56 effective when compounded monthly, 19.72 daily. Taking the limit as m grows without bound gives continuous compounding, where the effective rate is e raised to the r, minus one; at 18 percent nominal that is 19.72 percent, showing how quickly the limit is approached. Continuous compounding matters less in bank accounts than in modeling, where cash flows spread evenly through the year are often handled with continuous factors. The cardinal rule in all problems is to match the rate to the period: monthly payments require a monthly rate, and mixing a yearly rate with monthly periods is among the most common errors in practice. Inflation is the second translation problem. A dollar is a measuring rod that shrinks, with general price levels in the United States rising at a long-run average near 3 percent per year during the twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, so analyses must distinguish actual dollars, the inflated currency amounts that will actually change hands, from constant dollars, amounts expressed in the purchasing power of a base year. Each kind of dollar demands its own rate. Actual-dollar cash flows are discounted at the market rate; constant-dollar cash flows are discounted at the real, inflation-free rate. The two rates and the inflation rate f are linked by the Fisher relation, named for the economist Irving Fisher: one plus the market rate equals one plus the real rate, times one plus f. At a 10 percent market rate and 4 percent inflation, the real rate is 1.10 divided by 1.04, minus one, or 5.77 percent, not the 6 percent a naive subtraction gives, though the subtraction serves as an approximation when rates are small. Mixing the two systems, discounting constant dollars at a market rate, is a silent error that systematically punishes long-lived alternatives, because it double-counts inflation. It is depressingly common in practice. A correct analysis states its dollar convention in the first line, converts every figure to that convention, and applies the matching rate throughout, and a reviewer's first check should be exactly that consistency.

sections.heading: Present worth analysis and capitalized cost
sections.body: The present worth method is the workhorse decision criterion: convert every cash flow of an alternative to time zero at the MARR, sum them, and the result, the net present worth or net present value, states in today's dollars how much wealthier the alternative makes its owner than investing at the MARR would. A single project is acceptable if its present worth is zero or greater. Among mutually exclusive alternatives, the one with the largest present worth wins, costs counted negative, and for pure cost comparisons the least negative total wins. The method has one trap that invalidates more student and professional work than any other: alternatives must be compared over equal service lives. Comparing the present worth of a pump that lasts six years against one that lasts nine stacks nine years of service against six, and the shorter-lived machine is unfairly favored because its replacement costs fall outside the window. The standard remedies are three. First, compare over the least common multiple of the lives, here eighteen years, with each alternative repeated identically, which assumes replacements repeat at the same costs.
