Applied instead beneath a size dimension, to the axis of a pin or hole or the centre plane of a tab, straightness controls the derived median line, the string of midpoints of the feature's cross sections, requiring it to fit within a cylindrical zone of the stated diameter. Axis straightness is the standard way to permit a long pin to bow: under the American envelope principle a feature of size at maximum material condition must otherwise have perfect form, and an axis straightness tolerance is the explicit, deliberate override of that rule, the only form control allowed to breach the perfect-form envelope. It is routinely given with a maximum material condition modifier so that a slightly undersized pin may bow proportionally more, since what matters for assembly is the pin's virtual condition, its effective enlarged diameter when both size and bow are at their worst. A worked example makes the stakes concrete: a drive shaft 500 millimetres long at 19.98 to 20.00 millimetres diameter with an axis straightness of diameter 0.05 at maximum material condition has a virtual condition of 20.05 millimetres; any bearing bore of at least that diameter passes the shaft regardless of how the permitted size and bow combine, which is precisely the guarantee an assembler needs and precisely what no combination of size limits alone could promise.

sections.heading: Form tolerances: circularity and cylindricity
sections.body: Circularity, historically called roundness, controls each cross section of a round feature independently: at every position along a cylinder, cone, or sphere, the surface points in a plane perpendicular to the axis must lie between two concentric circles whose radii differ by the stated tolerance. Note the phrasing: the zone is an annular band on radius, so a circularity tolerance of 0.01 permits 0.01 millimetres of radial variation within a single cross section, and the standard is deliberately silent about how one cross section relates to the next; a cylinder could be perfectly round at every station yet taper or bow and still meet circularity. The control matters wherever a section must seal or run true against a mate: piston ring grooves, valve stems, bearing journals, O-ring glands. Its verification hides a genuinely subtle trap. The obvious check, spinning the part in a vee block under a dial indicator, superimposes the vee's own geometry on the reading and is blind to certain error shapes; a two-point diameter measurement with a micrometer is worse, because a surface can be built of constant-width lobes, like the British fifty-pence coin's heptagonal curve of constant width, that measure an identical diameter at every orientation while being visibly non-round. Three-lobed parts produced by centreless grinding classically show this behavior, measuring round to a micrometer while rattling in a true ring gauge. Rigorous circularity measurement therefore uses a rotating-spindle roundness instrument, in which the part or a gauge head spins on an air bearing an order of magnitude rounder than the tolerance being checked, and the standard association of the measured profile is a minimum-zone fit, the pair of concentric circles with the smallest radial separation containing the trace. Cylindricity is the three-dimensional composition: one tolerance zone, two coaxial cylinders whose radii differ by the stated value, containing the entire surface at once, thereby simultaneously limiting roundness of every section, straightness of every line element, and taper along the length. It is the strictest and most expensive of the form controls, appropriate for plunger bores, hydraulic cylinder walls, precision spool valves, and gauge pins, and it should be specified sparingly and verified with instruments equal to it, typically a roundness machine with a precision column allowing multiple stacked traces, or a dense coordinate measuring machine scan with minimum-zone evaluation software. Two cautions govern the whole family. First, form tolerances never take datum references and never locate anything; a perfectly cylindrical bore can still be in the wrong place, and pairing form controls with the location and orientation controls that need them is the designer's job, not the symbol's. Second, form interacts with surface texture: roughness in the micrometre range rides on top of form error, and on tight tolerances the drawing must make clear, through the governing standard's filtering defaults or explicit notes, how much of the fine texture the form measurement is meant to include, or two laboratories with different filter settings will honestly disagree about the same part.

sections.heading: Orientation tolerances: perpendicularity, parallelism, and angularity
sections.body: Orientation tolerances control the tilt of a feature relative to one or more datums without controlling its location. All three symbols in the family define the same kind of zone and differ only in the basic angle they enforce: perpendicularity for ninety degrees, parallelism for zero, and angularity for any other basic angle stated on the drawing. Applied to a flat surface, the tolerance defines two parallel planes separated by the stated value, perfectly oriented at the required angle to the datum, between which the entire surface must lie; because the real surface must fit inside an oriented slab, an orientation tolerance on a surface automatically limits its flatness to the same value, though not the reverse. Applied to an axis, usually with a diameter symbol, it defines a cylindrical zone perfectly oriented to the datum within which the axis must lie; a frame reading perpendicularity, diameter 0.05, to datum A on a pressed-in dowel hole means the hole's axis may lean by at most 0.05 millimetres over its own length relative to a perfect normal to the seating face. Be precise about what the number is: an orientation tolerance is a linear width, not an angle. The equivalent angle depends on the feature's length; 0.05 millimetres across a 50 millimetre face is about 0.057 degrees, while the same 0.05 across a 10 millimetre boss is five times coarser as an angle. This is why the linear form is used: mating parts feel displacements, not degrees, and stating the requirement as a width keeps it independent of feature size in exactly the way function is. Angularity requires the intended angle to appear as a basic dimension, in a box, with all permitted variation carried by the tolerance zone; writing forty-five degrees plus or minus half a degree instead creates a wedge-shaped zone that widens with distance from the vertex, an inferior, deprecated construction for anything functional. Common uses map straightforwardly to function: perpendicularity anchors bores that must stand square to mounting faces so that shafts do not run skewed, guides the squareness of fixture rails, and, applied to the datum features themselves, disciplines the secondary datum's squareness to the primary so the reference frame is trustworthy; parallelism holds the two faces of a spacer or gib so that clamping does not cock the stack, and holds a bore parallel to a mounting face in gearboxes where two shafts must not converge; angularity governs dovetails, chamfered seats, and inclined pads. Verification follows the zone definition: seat the datum feature on its simulator, then sweep the toleranced surface with an indicator whose travel is fixtured at the basic angle, or probe it and fit the oriented zone in software. Orientation frames may reference a secondary datum when tilt about the primary alone leaves a rotational ambiguity that function cares about. The family's limit must be kept in mind: none of these controls says where the feature is, and a bore can be perfectly square to a face while sitting millimetres from its intended location, so orientation tolerances usually work alongside position or profile, refining the orientation inside a location scheme.

sections.heading: Position: the workhorse control
sections.body: Position is the most used symbol in the system and the one that repays the deepest understanding. It controls how far the axis, centre plane, or centre point of a feature of size may stray from its theoretically exact location, which is defined by basic dimensions from a named datum reference frame. For a hole, the usual statement is a cylindrical zone: position, diameter 0.2, relative to A, B, C means the hole's axis must lie within a cylinder 0.2 millimetres in diameter whose own axis stands at the exact basic location, perpendicular to the primary datum, for the full depth of the hole. Because the zone is a cylinder through the part's thickness, position controls tilt of the hole as well as displacement, a fact often overlooked: a hole entering on location but leaning badly fails. The measured quantity behind the verdict is worth writing down. If a hole's actual axis position deviates from basic by dx in one direction and dy in the other, the diametral position deviation is two times the square root of dx squared plus dy squared, and the feature passes if that value does not exceed the zone diameter. The factor of two trips many newcomers: a hole off by 0.07 in x and 0.07 in y is displaced 0.099 radially and consumes 0.198 of a 0.2 zone, barely passing. Position also serves patterns, and there the datum logic earns its keep: all holes in a bolt circle are located by basic dimensions from the same frame, each with its own independent zone, so error does not accumulate around the circle the way chained coordinate dimensions accumulate it. The tolerance value itself should come from function, and for fastened joints there are standard formulas. For a floating fastener joint, where a bolt passes through clearance holes in two parts and a nut, each part's positional tolerance at maximum material condition may be as large as its hole's maximum material diameter minus the fastener's maximum diameter. For a fixed fastener joint, where the fastener threads into or is pressed into one member, the total available clearance must be shared, and the common allocation gives each part half: the tolerance equals hole maximum material diameter minus fastener diameter, divided between the clearance-hole part and the threaded part, often unequally when one is easier to make. A worked example: M6 bolts with 6.6 millimetre minimum clearance holes in both parts of a floating joint permit each part a positional tolerance of 0.6 millimetres diameter at maximum material condition, a startlingly generous number that honest functional analysis frequently produces. Position at regardless-of-feature-size is used where symmetry of material matters more than assembly, such as thin walls around a cored hole. Older drawings used concentricity and symmetry symbols for coaxial and symmetric relationships; the 2018 American standard deleted both in favor of position and runout, because their median-point definitions were expensive to measure and rarely matched function.

sections.heading: Material condition modifiers and bonus tolerance
sections.body: The circled M and circled L modifiers are where the language stops merely describing geometry and starts encoding assembly physics. A position tolerance followed by a circled M applies at maximum material condition: the stated zone is the guarantee when the feature is at its worst-case material state, the largest pin or smallest hole, and as the actual feature departs from that state toward least material, the zone grows by exactly the departure. The growth is called bonus tolerance. The reasoning is purely functional: what threatens assembly is the combination of material and mislocation; a hole drilled 0.1 millimetres larger than its minimum has donated 0.1 millimetres of extra clearance to the joint, and the fastener genuinely does not care whether that slack is spent on size or on location. Concretely, a hole dimensioned 10.0 to 10.2 with position diameter 0.2 at maximum material condition relative to A, B, C has a zone of 0.2 when the hole measures 10.0, a zone of 0.3 when it measures 10.1, and a zone of 0.4 at 10.2. The invariant behind the arithmetic is the virtual condition: for an internal feature it is the maximum material size minus the geometric tolerance at that size, here 10.0 minus 0.2 equals 9.8 millimetres, a fixed inner boundary that no combination of permitted size and permitted error will ever violate. A perfect pin of 9.8 millimetres at the true position will always pass through the hole; that pin, made physical, is a functional gauge, and the ability to verify parts with a simple hardened gauge instead of a coordinate measuring machine is the modifier's second gift, cutting inspection from minutes of programming to a two-second plug check on the shop floor. The circled L is the mirror image, applying the stated tolerance at least material condition with bonus accruing as the feature grows toward maximum material. It protects material where material is the concern rather than clearance: minimum wall thickness between a bore and an outside surface, minimum edge distance from a hole to a sheet edge, minimum machining stock on a casting datum. No modifier means regardless of feature size: the zone is constant, no bonus, appropriate for press fits, dowel holes that locate rather than merely clear, and kinematic interfaces where slop in a loose feature is not actually harmless. Modifiers may also follow datum references, and there the effect is different and differently named: a datum feature of size referenced at maximum material boundary allows datum shift, meaning the part as a whole may translate or rotate relative to the gauge by the clearance between the actual datum feature and its fixed-size virtual-condition simulator. Datum shift is not added to each feature's zone; it moves the whole reference frame, which can rescue a pattern that is uniformly offset but not one that is internally scattered. The discipline to remember: modifiers are chosen by function, clearance problems take M, material-thickness problems take L, and interchangeable-location problems take neither.

sections.heading: Profile tolerances: the universal control
sections.body: Profile of a surface is the most general tool in the box, able to control form alone, form plus orientation, or form plus orientation plus location, depending on whether and how datums are referenced, and it is the natural language for any shape that is not a plane or a cylinder: cast contours, aerofoil sections, moulded housings, sealing grooves, and increasingly, in model-based drawings, entire parts. The zone is a three-dimensional band shaped exactly like the theoretically exact surface defined by the model or by basic dimensions: by default the band straddles the true profile equally, extending half the tolerance to each side, so profile of a surface at 0.5 relative to A, B, C means every point of the real surface must lie within 0.25 millimetres of the exact nominal surface, measured normal to it, with the part constrained in the named frame. Unequal or entirely one-sided disposition is available when function is asymmetric, indicated in the modern American standard by the circled U modifier followed by the amount of tolerance lying outside the material: a casting that must always clean up in machining wants its profile band biased toward excess material, while a clearance contour that must never protrude wants the band held inside. Profile of a line is the two-dimensional sibling, applying the band independently to each cross section in a specified view, used where each section matters but the sections need not agree, as with extrusions and swept mouldings whose lengthwise variation is separately controlled. Without any datum reference, profile is a pure form control, a generalized flatness for curved surfaces. With datums, it locates: and this is the deep point, because a profile tolerance on a flat face referenced to a frame simultaneously controls that face's flatness, its orientation, and its distance from the datums, replacing what would otherwise be a flatness callout, a parallelism callout, and a toleranced dimension. Modern practice exploits this to produce drawings with one general profile note covering every surface not otherwise specified, with tighter frames only where function demands, a style that removes the last untoleranced surfaces from the definition and makes the model the single authority for nominal shape. Profile also supports composite frames in the same manner as position: an upper row locating the surface loosely to the assembly datums and a lower row holding the shape itself tightly, which suits, for example, a turbine blade whose aerofoil must be faithful in form to a few hundredths while its stacking position may float a few tenths. Verification is inherently computational for anything but simple shapes: a coordinate measuring machine or structured-light scanner probes the surface, software constrains the measurement to the datum frame, computes each point's normal deviation from nominal, and reports the extremes; hard gauging with contour templates and light-gap inspection against a radius gauge survives for simple sections and shop-floor triage. Because profile subsumes so much, its main hazard is thoughtless breadth: a blanket tight profile is a blanket cost, and the craft lies in a loose general profile with deliberate, justified refinement exactly where the function lives.

sections.heading: Runout: circular and total
sections.body: Runout is the family built for rotation, and it answers the question an assembler of shafts actually asks: when this part spins about its bearing axis, how much does this surface wobble? The datum for a runout tolerance is therefore always an axis, established from one cylindrical datum feature, from two separated journal surfaces acting together, as real shafts are supported in two bearings, or from a face and a short cylinder in combination. Circular runout, the single-arrow symbol, is checked one circular element at a time: the part is rotated exactly one revolution about the datum axis while a dial indicator rests on the surface at a fixed axial station, and the full indicator movement, the difference between the highest and lowest reading, must not exceed the tolerance at any station along the surface. Applied to a cylindrical surface it captures the combined effect of that section's eccentricity and its out-of-roundness in a single number, which is exactly the combination a seal lip or a gear mesh feels; applied to a shoulder face it captures the face's axial wobble. Total runout, the double-arrow symbol, raises the requirement: the indicator now traverses the entire surface while the part rotates, and every reading over the whole sweep must fall within the tolerance band. For a cylinder this simultaneously limits eccentricity, roundness error, straightness, and taper relative to the axis; for a face it simultaneously limits wobble and flatness, since the entire face must live between two planes perpendicular to the datum axis. Total runout is thus close to a rotation-referenced cylindricity plus coaxiality and is priced accordingly. Runout has two properties that make it beloved on the shop floor. It is defined directly in terms of an indicator measurement, so verification is fast, cheap, intuitive, and possible on a bench with centres or vee blocks supporting the datum journals; and it is a regardless-of-feature-size control by nature, never taking material condition modifiers, because a spinning assembly feels every micrometre of wobble no matter what size the feature happens to be. Its relationship to neighboring controls is worth keeping straight. Position at regardless of feature size applied to coaxial diameters controls the axis location but permits form error on top; circular runout is a stricter statement than mere coaxiality of an axis because surface error contributes; and the retired concentricity symbol demanded balance of diametrically opposed median points, an elegant but nearly unmeasurable idea that runout replaces in almost every practical case. Typical allocations on a machined drive shaft illustrate scale: bearing journals ground to a total runout of 0.01 to 0.02 millimetres relative to the common axis of the two journals, a seal surface at 0.05 circular runout so the lip is not slapped once per revolution, a flange face carrying a coupling at 0.02 total runout to avoid imposing a bending moment on the mating shaft, and non-functional clearance diameters left at ten times looser or uncontrolled. When balance, vibration, or sealing is the failure mode, runout is almost always the honest specification.

sections.heading: Verification: gauges, coordinate measuring machines, and honest measurement
sections.body: A tolerance means nothing until it can be verified, and the system was designed with verification inside it from the start. Verification splits into two philosophies. Attribute gauging asks a yes-or-no question with dedicated hardware: a functional gauge physically embodies the virtual condition of the toleranced features, a plate carrying hardened pins at the true positions, each pin at the hole pattern's virtual condition diameter, seated against the part's datum features in the specified order of precedence. If the part goes onto the gauge, the pattern passes; the gauge simultaneously checks every hole, includes bonus tolerance and datum shift automatically, costs seconds per part, and requires no skill to use, which is why maximum-material-condition tolerancing and functional gauging built the mass-production world. Its limits are symmetric: it gives no number, so it cannot feed process control charts or tell you how close to the edge the process is running, it cannot check regardless-of-feature-size or least-material requirements, and the gauge itself must be made ten times more accurately than the tolerance it checks, the traditional gauge-maker's rule of ten. Variable measurement produces numbers. The dominant instrument is the coordinate measuring machine, a bridge or arm carrying a touch-trigger or scanning probe whose tip position is known to a stated maximum permissible error, commonly a few micrometres plus a length-dependent term, expressed in the form of E equals 1.7 plus L over 300 micrometres under the ISO 10360 family of acceptance tests. The machine samples points on each feature, software associates ideal geometry with the point clouds, constructs the datum reference frame mathematically, and evaluates each frame on the drawing. Here honest measurement demands attention to three details that silently change answers. Sampling: five points on a bore is a legal circle fit but blind to three-lobed error; standards-aware laboratories set point counts and distributions to match the feature's expected error shapes. Association: fitting a plane by least squares gives a different datum than the high-point contact a physical surface plate makes, and the American standard's datum definition is the contacting exterior plane, so software must be told to simulate contact, not regression, when correspondence with hard gauging matters. Filtering: scanned data includes roughness that a plug gauge never feels, and filter settings decide how much of it counts. Beyond these, every laboratory must reckon with measurement uncertainty: a 0.02 millimetre tolerance checked by a process with 0.005 of expanded uncertainty leaves a decision zone in which parts can be neither confidently accepted nor rejected, and standard practice, formalized in ISO 14253, is to guard-band, accepting only parts measured inside the tolerance by at least the uncertainty. Simpler instruments retain their place in this hierarchy: surface plates, gauge blocks calibrated in grades traceable to the metre, height gauges, sine bars for angles, air gauges for tight bores at high volume, and optical comparators for profiles. The craft is matching instrument to tolerance, with capability comfortably better than the requirement, and recording enough of the setup that a second laboratory can reproduce the verdict.

sections.heading: Applying the system to a real part
sections.body: Tolerancing is done well only in one direction: from function backward to numbers, never from habit or from what the shop did last time. The working method below suits a typical machined or moulded component that mounts to something, locates on something, and passes or carries other parts. Begin by interrogating the assembly, not the part: every functional requirement, fit, seal, alignment, clearance, is a relationship between two parts, and the tolerances exist to guarantee those relationships. The datum reference frame comes first because everything else hangs on it, and it should mirror the physical assembly sequence: the surface that seats first is primary, the feature that locates next is secondary. Only then are individual feature tolerances chosen, and each should be the largest value that analysis shows still guarantees the function, because every unnecessary halving of a tolerance is a multiplication of cost. For fastened patterns, apply the fixed and floating fastener formulas; for stacked clearances, sum a worst-case chain first, and only relax to a statistical root-sum-square model, in which the expected stack is the square root of the sum of squared individual tolerances, when production volumes and process control genuinely justify betting on variation averaging out. Check every tolerance against the process: a value tighter than roughly 0.1 millimetres will usually push a part from moulding or stamping into machining, tighter than 0.02 into grinding, tighter than 0.005 into lapping or honing, each jump roughly doubling to quadrupling the operation's cost, and a tolerance the measuring room cannot verify with comfortable margin is not a specification but a wish. Finally, walk the finished drawing as three strangers: the machinist deciding how to fixture, the gauge maker deciding what to build, and a lawyer deciding whether a disputed part passes.
steps: 1. List every functional requirement of the part as a relationship with a mating part: what must fit, seal, align, rotate, or clear, and by how much.
2. Choose datum features that mirror how the part actually seats and locates in the assembly, and order them primary, secondary, tertiary by contact sequence.
3. Qualify the datum features themselves with form and orientation tolerances so the reference frame is trustworthy.
4. Locate every functional feature of size with basic dimensions from the frame and a position tolerance; compute fastener-joint values with the fixed or floating fastener formula.
5. Add maximum material modifiers where the requirement is assembly clearance, least material where it is minimum wall or edge material, and neither where location itself is the function.
6. Cover remaining surfaces with a general profile tolerance referenced to the frame, refining only where function demands more.
7. Run worst-case stack calculations across every critical chain; relax to statistical stacks only with demonstrated process control.
8. Verify each tolerance is achievable by the intended process and measurable by available instruments with at least a four-to-one capability margin.
9. Review the drawing from the machinist's, gauge maker's, and inspector's viewpoints, and remove every requirement you cannot justify functionally.

sections.heading: Common mistakes, limits, and when parts still fail
sections.body: The system fails most often at the hands of its users, and the failure patterns are stable enough to catalogue. The commonest is the missing or meaningless datum: a position tolerance with no datum references, or referenced to a datum letter defined on a tiny cosmetic chamfer that cannot physically constrain the part, or three datums that do not arrest six degrees of freedom, leaving the inspector to improvise the missing constraint differently every time. Next is over-tolerancing, the reflexive tight number: a 0.01 flatness on a face that merely keeps dirt out multiplies cost invisibly, and drawings salted with unjustified precision teach suppliers to ignore all of it, including the values that matter. Its mirror is the untoleranced escape: a surface controlled by nothing, legal under older drafting habits, which becomes whatever the process makes it. Misused modifiers recur: maximum material condition on a press-fit dowel hole, quietly permitting located slop exactly where the design needed none, or bonus tolerance claimed on a datum reference as if it enlarged each feature's zone rather than shifting the whole frame. Inspection introduces its own failures: measuring flatness as parallelism to the inspection table, fitting datums by least squares when the definition demands high-point contact, sampling five points on a lobed bore, or reporting a measured value with an uncertainty larger than the tolerance and calling the part good. And there are genuine limits of the language itself. It presumes rigidity; sheet metal, plastics, and gaskets deform under gravity and clamping, and for them the standard permits restrained-state specifications, in which the drawing states the fixturing forces and constraint points under which the tolerances apply, with the circled F marking requirements that must hold in the free state. It defines acceptance, not process: a drawing says what passes, and says nothing about how a shop should centre and stabilize its process to make passing routine; that gap is filled by process capability statistics, where a capability index of 1.33, meaning the tolerance spans at least eight standard deviations of the process centred within it, is the customary minimum for critical features. It also cannot rescue a bad scheme: if the datum features chosen do not match how the part truly seats, every measurement downstream is a well-defined answer to the wrong question, and parts will measure good and assemble badly, the signature symptom of a functional datum error. When such a failure appears, the diagnostic path is fixed: first confirm the measurement reproduces between laboratories, then check the drawing's datum scheme against the physical assembly, then check the stack arithmetic against the worst case actually manufactured, and only then suspect the process. Treated with that discipline, the language does what it was invented to do in 1938: it lets strangers who never meet make parts that fit together the first time, and gives every dispute about quality a numerical answer instead of an argument.

guides.title: Statics: forces and equilibrium in structures
guides.summary: A complete working introduction to statics, the branch of mechanics that explains why structures stand still: forces, moments, supports, trusses, beams, arches, friction, buckling and the failure modes that follow when equilibrium is misjudged.

sections.heading: Why nothing standing still is actually simple
sections.body:
A bridge that carries ten thousand vehicles a day and never moves looks like the least interesting object in engineering. It is in fact a machine holding a precise draw with itself. Every kilogram of steel and concrete is pulling downward under gravity, every wheel that rolls across it adds a travelling load, wind pushes sideways, the sun heats one face and makes it try to grow longer than the other, and yet the deck stays within a few millimetres of where the drawings said it would be. Statics is the body of reasoning that explains how that stalemate is arranged, and more usefully, how to arrange it deliberately rather than by luck.

The word comes from the Greek statikos, meaning causing to stand. The subject is the study of bodies that are not accelerating. That sounds like a narrow special case, but it covers the overwhelming majority of the built world: buildings, bridges, dams, towers, retaining walls, aircraft parked on a ramp, a bookshelf, a ladder against a wall, a tent guyed against a gale. It also covers anything moving at constant velocity, because constant velocity means zero acceleration too. A lift travelling smoothly upward at two metres per second is a statics problem; only the moments of starting and stopping are not.

The intellectual heart of the subject is a single idea inherited from Isaac Newton's second law of 1687. Force equals mass times acceleration. If acceleration is zero, then the sum of forces must be zero. Extend that to rotation and you get the second condition: the sum of turning effects, called moments, must also be zero, otherwise the object would spin up. Everything else in statics — every truss analysis, every beam diagram, every foundation calculation — is bookkeeping applied to those two statements. The difficulty is never the physics. It is the accounting: identifying every force acting on the piece you are studying, without inventing one that does not exist and without quietly forgetting one that does.

That accounting discipline is why statics is taught before anything else in structural engineering, and why it repays study even for someone who will never design a building. It gives you a reliable way to answer the practical questions that recur constantly. Will this shelf hold? Where should the prop go? Why did the ladder slip? How heavy can the load on that roof beam get before something bad happens, and what exactly is the bad thing? Which member of this frame is doing the real work, and which is along for the ride? A person who can draw a correct free body diagram and balance forces and moments on it has a genuine engineering skill, one that transfers from a timber roof to a rope rigging system to a shelf bracket without changing a single principle.

sections.heading: Force as a vector, and the free body diagram
sections.body:
A force is a push or a pull, and the crucial thing about it is that it has both size and direction. Quantities with both are called vectors, and they cannot be added like ordinary numbers. Two forces of 100 newtons each, pulling in the same direction, give 200 newtons. The same two pulling in opposite directions give zero. Pulling at right angles to each other they give about 141 newtons, because vectors combine by the parallelogram rule, which in the right-angle case reduces to Pythagoras: the square root of one hundred squared plus one hundred squared. Getting this right is the first hurdle, and most beginner errors in statics are ultimately vector arithmetic errors dressed up as something else.

The working unit is the newton, defined as the force that accelerates one kilogram at one metre per second squared. On Earth's surface, gravity accelerates objects at roughly 9.81 metres per second squared, so a one kilogram mass weighs about 9.81 newtons, and a convenient rough conversion is that a kilogram weighs about ten newtons. A person of 80 kilograms therefore presses down with roughly 785 newtons. A tonne of material weighs about 9.81 kilonewtons. Engineers work in kilonewtons constantly because the numbers stay manageable: a small house might weigh 1,500 kilonewtons in total.

Rather than juggle vectors geometrically, it is almost always easier to split each force into components along two perpendicular axes, conventionally horizontal and vertical, and treat each axis separately. A force of magnitude F acting at an angle of theta above the horizontal has a horizontal component F times the cosine of theta and a vertical component F times the sine of theta. A 500 newton rope pull at 30 degrees above horizontal therefore contributes 433 newtons horizontally and 250 newtons vertically. Two independent columns of arithmetic replace one awkward geometry problem.

The single most valuable habit in the whole subject is the free body diagram. You choose a body — the whole structure, one beam, one joint, one bolt, half of a bridge cut with an imaginary knife — and you draw it in isolation, removed from everything it touches. Then you replace each thing you removed with the force it was exerting. The ground becomes an upward reaction. The wall becomes a horizontal push and possibly a friction force. A rope becomes a pull along its own line, never a push, because ropes cannot push. Gravity becomes a single downward arrow at the centre of gravity.

Every force on the diagram must have a physical source you can name and point to. If you cannot say what object is applying an arrow, that arrow is wrong. Conversely, if the body touches something and you have drawn no arrow there, you have almost certainly lost a force. Draw the diagram badly and no amount of later algebra will save the answer; draw it correctly and the algebra is usually trivial.

sections.heading: The equilibrium equations and what they assert
sections.body:
For a body that is not accelerating in a flat, two-dimensional problem, three equations must hold simultaneously. The sum of all horizontal force components equals zero. The sum of all vertical force components equals zero. And the sum of all moments about any chosen point equals zero. Written compactly these are the equations of static equilibrium, and they are the entire toolkit. In three dimensions there are six equations instead: three force sums along three axes and three moment sums about three axes.

The first two are intuitive. If more force pushes right than left, the object accelerates rightward, so it is not static. If the upward reactions do not add up to the downward weights, the thing either sinks or flies. Take a shelf carrying a 200 newton load, held by two brackets. Vertical equilibrium says the two bracket forces must sum to 200 newtons plus the shelf's own weight. Nothing about how the load splits between them yet, only that the total is fixed.

The third equation, the moment condition, is what makes statics powerful, because it is what tells you the split. A moment is a force multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the point you are taking moments about to the line along which the force acts. That perpendicular distance is called the lever arm. Its units are newton metres. A 200 newton load sitting 0.3 metres from a bracket produces a moment of 60 newton metres about that bracket.

The subtle and enormously useful property of the moment equation is that you may take moments about any point at all, including points outside the object, and it must still balance. This is a gift, because choosing the point wisely makes unknown forces vanish. Any force whose line of action passes through your chosen point has zero lever arm and therefore contributes zero moment. So if you take moments about one bracket, that bracket's own unknown reaction drops out of the equation entirely, and the remaining equation contains only one unknown, which you can solve directly. This trick — take moments about the point where an inconvenient unknown acts — is the single most used manoeuvre in the subject.

A worked case makes it concrete. A uniform plank 4 metres long weighing 300 newtons rests on supports at each end. A person of 700 newtons stands 1 metre from the left support. Take moments about the left support. The person contributes 700 times 1, which is 700 newton metres clockwise. The plank's own weight acts at its centre, 2 metres along, contributing 300 times 2, or 600 newton metres clockwise. The right reaction acts 4 metres away, anticlockwise, contributing R times 4. Balance gives 4R equal to 1,300, so R equals 325 newtons. Vertical equilibrium then gives the left reaction as 1,000 minus 325, which is 675 newtons. Two equations, complete answer.

sections.heading: Moments, levers, and couples
sections.body:
The moment of a force is the measure of its tendency to rotate a body about a point or an axis. Archimedes understood the principle in the third century BC well enough to claim that with a long enough lever and a place to stand he could move the Earth, and the arithmetic behind that boast is exactly the arithmetic used to size a crane today. Moment equals force multiplied by perpendicular distance. Double the distance and you double the turning effect for the same effort. This is why a long spanner loosens a seized nut that a short one will not, why a wheelbarrow with a long handle carries a heavy load comfortably, and why the outstretched arm of a tower crane needs a counterweight over its tail.

The word perpendicular in that definition carries all the weight. The lever arm is not the distance to the point where the force is applied; it is the shortest distance from the pivot to the infinite straight line along which the force acts. If you push a door at its handle but directly toward the hinge, the line of action passes through the hinge, the perpendicular distance is zero, and the door does not swing however hard you push. Push at right angles to the door and the lever arm equals the full width, giving the maximum effect. At intermediate angles the effective moment is force times distance times the sine of the angle between them.

Sign convention matters. Pick one rotational direction as positive — anticlockwise is the common choice — and stay with it through every equation in a problem. Mixing conventions midway is a common source of a wrong answer that looks plausible.

A special and important case is the couple: two equal forces acting in opposite directions along parallel but different lines. Their vector sum is zero, so they cannot push a body anywhere, but their moments add rather than cancel, so they produce pure rotation. The two hands on a steering wheel form a couple. A screwdriver's grip forms a couple. Critically, the moment of a couple is the same about every point in the plane, equal to one force multiplied by the perpendicular gap between the two lines. It is a free vector, and this property is what allows engineers to speak of an applied torque at a point without specifying exactly where the forces creating it act.

In structures, the moment concept has a second life as an internal quantity. Cut through a loaded beam and the two halves are exchanging not only a shear force but a bending moment, the internal couple that resists the beam's tendency to fold. This internal bending moment is what actually sizes most beams: the top of the beam is being squeezed, the bottom is being stretched, and the further apart the material sits from the neutral middle, the more moment it can resist for the same amount of steel or timber. That single insight is why an I-beam concentrates its material in flanges top and bottom rather than distributing it evenly.

sections.heading: Supports and reactions: how a structure is held
sections.body:
A structure interacts with the ground and with its neighbours through supports, and the whole art of setting up a statics problem lies in translating a real physical connection into the right idealised support. Each idealisation says exactly which movements the connection prevents, and the rule is direct: a support supplies a reaction force in every direction it prevents movement, and a reaction moment if it prevents rotation.

The roller support prevents movement in one direction only, usually vertical, and supplies a single reaction perpendicular to the surface it rolls on. It permits sliding along the surface and permits rotation. Real examples include a beam resting on a greased bearing plate, the sliding end of a bridge deck sitting on elastomeric pads, or a joist simply lying on a wall with nothing fixing it. Bridges very deliberately use rollers or sliding bearings at one end so the deck can lengthen and shorten with temperature. A 100 metre steel span heated by 30 degrees grows about 36 millimetres, and a structure that forbids that growth will instead generate enormous internal forces trying to accommodate it.

The pin or hinge support prevents movement in both horizontal and vertical directions but allows free rotation. It therefore supplies two unknown reaction components and no moment. A bolted connection through a single pin, a door hinge, and the classic bridge bearing at the fixed end are all pins. Because it resists two directions, a pin plus a roller is the minimum arrangement that holds a simple beam completely.

The fixed or built-in support prevents everything: horizontal movement, vertical movement, and rotation. It therefore supplies three unknowns, two force components and a reaction moment. A steel column welded to a heavy base plate that is itself bolted deep into a concrete foundation approximates a fixed support. So does a cantilevered balcony cast monolithically into a floor slab, or a fence post concreted into the ground. A flagpole is a fixed support carrying a vertical cantilever, and the moment at its base is what usually governs the design.

Cables and ties form a fourth category. A cable can only pull, never push, and the force must lie along the cable's own line. Guy wires on a mast, tent guy lines, and hanger rods in a suspension bridge all obey this. If your analysis returns a negative value for a cable force, meaning compression, the honest conclusion is not a small negative number but that the cable has gone slack and is doing nothing at all, and the whole analysis must be redone without it.

Getting the idealisation wrong shifts forces to places you did not calculate. Assuming a pin where the real connection is nearly rigid underestimates the moment the connection actually attracts, and welded joints have failed for exactly that reason. Assuming rigidity where the connection is really flexible overestimates it and can leave the member itself under-designed.

sections.heading: Determinacy, indeterminacy and stability
sections.body:
Once supports are chosen, a counting question decides whether simple equilibrium can solve the structure at all. In a plane problem you have three equations. If the supports introduce exactly three unknown reactions, the structure is statically determinate and you can find every reaction from equilibrium alone, with no knowledge whatsoever of what the structure is made of. A simply supported beam with a pin at one end (two unknowns) and a roller at the other (one unknown) is the canonical example. So is a cantilever with a single fixed support supplying three unknowns.

If the supports introduce fewer than three unknowns, the structure is a mechanism. It cannot be held. Three rollers on flat ground supply three vertical reactions but nothing to resist a horizontal push, so the structure slides away. Counting is necessary but not sufficient: the arrangement matters as much as the number. Three parallel reactions can never balance a force across them, and three reactions whose lines of action all meet at a single point can never balance a moment about that point. Both configurations are geometrically unstable despite passing the count, and both have caused real collapses in temporary works, where props are placed by number rather than by geometry.

If the supports introduce more than three unknowns, the structure is statically indeterminate, or redundant. A beam with a pin at each end has four unknowns; a beam on three supports has four; a portal frame fixed at both feet has six. Equilibrium still holds, but it no longer supplies enough equations to find every unknown. The missing information is supplied by how much the structure deforms, which depends on the stiffness of every member: its material, its cross-section, its length. Solving these problems requires compatibility conditions in addition to equilibrium, and in practice a computer running a stiffness-matrix analysis.

Redundancy is not a defect, and modern design deliberately embraces it. An indeterminate structure has alternative load paths. If one member is damaged, forces can redistribute rather than the whole thing coming down, and this quality is called robustness. The 1968 partial collapse of Ronan Point in east London, where a domestic gas explosion on the eighteenth floor blew out a load-bearing panel and the corner of the block progressively fell, drove exactly this lesson into building codes worldwide: structures must be tied together so that the loss of one element does not propagate.

The cost of redundancy is sensitivity. Because forces in an indeterminate structure depend on relative stiffnesses, they also depend on things a determinate structure ignores entirely: temperature change, foundation settlement, shrinkage of concrete, and errors in fabricated length. A continuous beam over three supports will develop real, sometimes large, internal forces if the middle support settles by twenty millimetres, whereas a determinate pair of simple beams would simply tilt and carry on. Designers of long structures on soft or variable ground often choose determinacy for exactly this reason.

sections.heading: Trusses and the method of joints
sections.body:
A truss is a framework of straight members connected at their ends to form a set of triangles. The triangle is the only polygon whose shape cannot change without changing the length of a side, which is why a triangulated frame is stiff while a rectangle of four pinned bars folds flat like a parallelogram unless something braces it diagonally. Roof trusses, lattice bridge girders, transmission towers, crane jibs, scaffolding towers and geodesic domes are all applications of this one geometric fact.

Classical truss analysis rests on three idealising assumptions, and they are worth stating because each is slightly false in reality. First, all members are joined by frictionless pins, so joints transmit force but not moment. Second, all loads are applied only at the joints, not partway along a member. Third, every member's centreline passes exactly through the joint centre. Under these assumptions each member carries only an axial force, pure tension or pure compression along its own length, and nothing else. Real trusses are welded or bolted, which introduces some joint fixity and small secondary bending stresses, generally under about ten per cent of the axial stress and conventionally neglected in ordinary work.

The method of joints exploits the fact that every pin joint is itself a body in equilibrium, acted upon only by concurrent forces meeting at a point. Because all the forces pass through the same point, no moments arise, and only two equations apply at each joint: horizontal sum zero and vertical sum zero. Two equations solve at most two unknowns, so the procedure is to find the external reactions first from overall equilibrium, then start at a joint where only two member forces are unknown and work outward joint by joint.

The sign convention that makes this manageable is to assume every unknown member force is tension, drawn as an arrow pulling away from the joint. If the algebra returns a positive number, the member really is in tension. If it returns a negative number, the member is in compression, and there is no need to redraw anything. Once a member's force is known at one end, it is known at the other, so it feeds directly into the next joint.

Consider a symmetric roof truss spanning 12 metres with a 3 metre rise, supporting 20 kilonewtons at the apex and pinned at one support with a roller at the other. Symmetry gives each reaction as 10 kilonewtons upward. At the left support joint, the rafter runs up at an angle whose tangent is 3 divided by 6, so about 26.6 degrees, with sine 0.447. Vertical equilibrium at that joint requires the rafter's vertical component to balance 10 kilonewtons upward, so the rafter force is 10 divided by 0.447, or 22.4 kilonewtons compression. Horizontal equilibrium then gives the bottom tie a tension of 22.4 times cosine 26.6, which is 20 kilonewtons. The bottom chord is a tie being pulled hard, and it is that outward thrust which a masonry wall beneath a badly detailed roof is often unable to resist.

sections.heading: The method of sections and zero-force members
sections.body:
Working joint by joint through a forty-member bridge truss to find the force in one member near the middle is tedious and error-prone, because an arithmetic slip early on contaminates everything downstream. The method of sections avoids this. Instead of isolating a joint, you cut an imaginary line straight through the truss, slicing through the members you are interested in, and treat everything on one side of the cut as a single rigid body.

That body is in equilibrium like any other, so the full three equations apply: horizontal sum, vertical sum, and moment sum about any point. The forces exposed at the cut are the axial forces in the severed members. Because there are three equations, a cut through three unknown members can be solved completely, and a well-chosen moment centre often gives one member's force in a single line of arithmetic.

The moment centre trick is the key to efficiency. To find a top chord force, take moments about the joint where the two other cut members meet, so both drop out and only the chord remains. To find a diagonal's force in a parallel-chord truss, use vertical equilibrium, because the horizontal chords contribute nothing vertically and the diagonal alone must carry the shear across the cut. Practised engineers can read a Warren or Pratt truss almost by inspection using these two moves: chords resist the overall bending, so they grow toward midspan; diagonals resist shear, so they grow toward the supports.

A related labour-saving idea is the zero-force member, which carries no load under a given loading and can be identified by inspection before any calculation. Two rules cover almost all cases. First, if a joint connects exactly two members that are not collinear, and no external load or reaction acts at that joint, both members carry zero force, because there is nothing to balance either one's component perpendicular to the other. Second, if a joint connects three members of which two are collinear, and no external load acts there, the odd third member carries zero force, since nothing balances its perpendicular component.

Zero-force members are not useless, which is a common misreading. They carry nothing under this particular load case but may be essential under another, such as wind from the opposite direction or an asymmetric snow drift. They also brace long compression members against buckling by shortening their unsupported length, a service that never appears in an axial force calculation but which routinely governs whether a slender strut survives. Removing a member because one analysis showed zero force in it has caused failures.

Both methods can be combined freely in one problem: a section cut to leap across the structure to the region of interest, then joints worked locally from there. Nothing in the physics distinguishes them; they are two ways of choosing the free body, and choosing the free body well is most of the skill.

sections.heading: Beams: shear force and bending moment
sections.body:
A beam is a member loaded across its length rather than along it, and it is the workhorse of construction: floor joists, lintels over windows, bridge girders, aircraft wing spars, and the axle of a trailer are all beams. Understanding one requires looking inside it, because the interesting quantities are internal. Cut the beam anywhere and ask what the two halves must exchange to keep each half in equilibrium. The answer is generally two things: a shear force acting across the cut, which stops one half sliding past the other, and a bending moment, an internal couple that stops one half rotating relative to the other.

Shear force at any cross-section equals the algebraic sum of all vertical forces on one side of it. Bending moment at that section equals the sum of the moments of those same forces about the section. Plot each along the beam and you get the shear force diagram and the bending moment diagram, the two drawings that dominate practical beam design, because between them they tell you where the beam is working hardest and by how much.

Several relationships make these diagrams quick to draw. The slope of the shear diagram at any point equals the negative of the distributed load intensity there. The slope of the bending moment diagram equals the shear. It follows that bending moment reaches a maximum exactly where shear crosses zero, which is the single most useful fact in beam work: find where shear passes through zero and you have found where the beam is most likely to break in bending. A point load produces a sudden step in the shear diagram and a sharp kink in the moment diagram. A uniform load produces a straight sloping shear line and a parabolic moment curve.

The standard cases are worth memorising because they recur endlessly. A simply supported beam of span L carrying a total uniformly distributed load w per unit length has maximum shear of wL divided by 2 at each support, and maximum bending moment of w L squared divided by 8 at midspan. The same beam with a single point load P at midspan has maximum shear P over 2 and maximum moment PL over 4. A cantilever of length L with a point load P at the free end has maximum moment PL, at the fixed root, and a cantilever with uniform load has maximum moment w L squared over 2, also at the root.

Those formulas carry a design lesson embedded in the algebra. Bending moment scales with the square of span. Double a floor joist's span and, for the same load per metre, the bending moment quadruples. That is why extending a span is so much more expensive than it looks, and why an extra intermediate support, or a beam under the middle of a long joist run, is so disproportionately effective. Halving the span cuts the required strength to a quarter.

sections.heading: From force to stress: sizing the material
sections.body:
Equilibrium tells you how big the internal forces are. It says nothing about whether the material can take them. That step requires stress, defined as force divided by the area carrying it, measured in pascals, where one pascal is one newton per square metre. Because a pascal is tiny, structural work uses megapascals, and one megapascal is exactly one newton per square millimetre, a coincidence that makes mental arithmetic pleasant: a 50 kilonewton tension in a bar of 500 square millimetres cross-section gives 100 megapascals.

Typical strengths anchor the scale. Ordinary structural steel yields at about 275 to 355 megapascals and has a Young's modulus of 200 gigapascals. Aluminium alloy yields around 150 to 300 megapascals with a modulus of 70 gigapascals, so it stretches nearly three times as much as steel for the same stress. Softwood timber loaded along the grain manages roughly 7 to 20 megapascals in bending but only about 0.5 megapascals across the grain in shear. Concrete is strong in compression at 25 to 50 megapascals and effectively worthless in tension, which is precisely why steel reinforcement is placed on the tension face.

Strain is the companion quantity: the change in length divided by the original length, a pure ratio with no units. Robert Hooke's 1678 law states that for elastic materials stress is proportional to strain, and the constant of proportionality is Young's modulus, E. Rearranged, the extension of a bar equals force times length divided by area times modulus. A steel tie 3 metres long with a 400 square millimetre section carrying 80 kilonewtons stretches by 80,000 times 3,000 divided by 400 times 200,000, which is 3 millimetres. That small number matters: deflection limits, not strength, govern a great many floor beams.

Bending stress is distributed rather than uniform. In a beam bending downward, the top fibres shorten and the bottom fibres lengthen, and somewhere between lies the neutral axis, where stress is zero. Stress grows linearly with distance from that axis, so the extreme fibres carry the most. The governing formula is that maximum bending stress equals bending moment divided by the section modulus, written M over Z. Section modulus depends only on the shape of the cross-section. For a rectangle of breadth b and depth d, Z equals b d squared over 6.

The d squared is the whole reason a joist is laid on edge rather than flat. A 50 by 200 millimetre timber on edge has a section modulus of 50 times 200 squared over 6, which is 333,000 cubic millimetres. Laid flat the same piece gives 200 times 50 squared over 6, or 83,300 — exactly four times weaker, from the same material, for free. Steel I-sections take this to its logical end, putting the metal in flanges as far from the neutral axis as buckling of the thin web will permit.

sections.heading: Arches, cables and funicular form
sections.body:
Some structures achieve equilibrium not by resisting bending but by avoiding it, adopting a shape in which the loads are carried by pure tension or pure compression along the member's own line. Such a shape is called funicular, from the Latin for rope, and finding it is one of the most elegant ideas in structural engineering.

Hang a chain freely between two points and it settles into a curve called a catenary, mathematically a hyperbolic cosine. Every element of the chain is in pure tension; a chain cannot resist bending, so it has no choice but to find the shape in which none is required. Change the loading and the shape changes with it: a cable carrying a load spread evenly along the horizontal, as in a suspension bridge deck hung from many closely spaced hangers, takes a parabola rather than a catenary. The two curves are close but not identical, and for the very long spans of a bridge like the 1998 Akashi Kaikyo, with its 1,991 metre main span, the distinction is real engineering.

Robert Hooke stated the corresponding principle for compression in 1675, publishing it as a Latin anagram and revealing the solution only after his death: as hangs the flexible line, so but inverted will stand the rigid arch. Invert the tension curve and you get the ideal compression curve for the same loading. Antoni Gaudi built physical hanging-chain models weighted with small bags of shot for the Colonia Guell chapel, photographed them, and turned the photographs upside down to obtain his arch geometry. Modern computers do the same calculation, but the physical method remains exactly correct.

The practical consequence is thrust. An arch does not push straight down on its supports; it pushes outward and downward along the tangent of its curve. A masonry arch of span S and rise r carrying total load W generates a horizontal thrust of roughly W S divided by 8 r. A shallow arch, with small r, generates enormous thrust. This is why Gothic cathedrals grew flying buttresses, why a Roman aqueduct's piers are so massive, and why a modern tied arch bridge runs a steel tie across the bottom to swallow the thrust internally rather than passing it to the foundations.

Masonry arches carry a further subtlety. Because mortar cannot be relied on in tension, an arch stands only if a line of thrust — the geometric path traced by the resultant compressive force — can be drawn that stays inside the masonry everywhere. Jacques Heyman formalised this as the safe theorem: if any statically admissible thrust line fits within the material, the arch is safe, regardless of which one it actually follows. That is why old arches survive settlement and cracking that would seem alarming. The arch simply finds a new thrust line. It fails only when no admissible line fits, which typically means four hinges have formed and the arch has become a mechanism.

sections.heading: Friction, wedges and self-locking
sections.body:
Friction is the tangential resistance that arises when two surfaces are pressed together and one tries to slide over the other. It is unglamorous and slightly disreputable in engineering, because its magnitude is uncertain and variable, yet nothing built could stand without it. The rungs of a ladder against a wall, the grip of a bolt, the stability of a gravel slope, the ability to walk across a floor, and the way a masonry wall resists sliding under wind all depend on it.

Charles-Augustin de Coulomb's 1785 model remains the working description. The friction force available is proportional to the normal force pressing the surfaces together, with the constant of proportionality called the coefficient of friction, mu. Crucially, friction is a passive force: it supplies exactly as much resistance as is required to prevent sliding, up to a maximum of mu times the normal force. Below that limit it takes whatever value equilibrium demands. Above it, the surfaces slide, and the coefficient drops slightly to a kinetic value, which is why an object that starts to slip tends to accelerate rather than settle.

Representative values are worth carrying in memory, with the honest caveat that they scatter widely with surface finish, contamination and moisture. Steel on dry steel is around 0.6, dropping to 0.1 or below when lubricated. Rubber on dry asphalt is around 0.7 to 0.9 and can fall below 0.2 on ice. Wood on wood is about 0.3 to 0.5. Timber ladder feet on a smooth wet tile floor may be under 0.2, which is precisely the arrangement in which ladders slide out.

Because friction depends on the normal force, its available magnitude is coupled to the rest of the equilibrium problem, which produces some non-intuitive results. Consider a uniform ladder of weight W leaning at angle theta against a frictionless wall, with friction only at the floor. Taking moments about the top and resolving gives the condition for the ladder not to slip: the tangent of theta must be at least 1 divided by twice mu. With mu equal to 0.3, tan theta must exceed 1.67, meaning the ladder must be steeper than about 59 degrees. The common builder's rule of one unit out for four units up gives about 76 degrees, a comfortable margin. Note that the ladder's own weight cancels out entirely, so a heavier ladder is no safer, but a person standing near the top shifts the effective weight upward and makes slipping easier, which is why the rule tightens for work at height.

The friction angle, defined as the arctangent of mu, gives a compact criterion: if the resultant force between two surfaces lies within a cone of that half-angle about the normal, no sliding occurs. Wedges, screw threads and taper joints exploit this to be self-locking, holding their position without any external restraint, which is why a screw does not unwind and a splitting wedge stays in the log.

sections.heading: Centre of gravity and overturning
sections.body:
The centre of gravity is the single point at which the entire weight of a body may be considered to act. For statics purposes it is identical to the centroid whenever the material density is uniform, and the centroid is a purely geometric property: the average position of all the area or volume. For a rectangle it is at the intersection of the diagonals. For a triangle it lies one third of the way up from the base toward the apex, on the median. For a semicircle of radius R the centroid sits 4R divided by 3 pi from the flat edge, roughly 0.424R.

Composite shapes are handled by dividing them into simple parts, multiplying each part's area by the distance of its own centroid from a chosen reference line, adding those products, and dividing by the total area. Holes and cut-outs are included as negative areas. An L-shaped concrete footing, a stepped retaining wall, and an asymmetric steel section are all handled this way in a few lines of arithmetic.

Overturning is the failure mode that centre of gravity governs, and it is disarmingly simple: an object tips when the vertical line through its centre of gravity falls outside the base of support. Nothing else is required for the criterion, which is why it applies equally to a filing cabinet, a crane, a retaining wall and a person standing on a moving bus. Widen the base or lower the centre of gravity and stability improves. A Formula One car is stable at speed for the same reason a wine glass is not.

Engineers express this as a factor of safety against overturning: the restoring moment about the likely tipping edge divided by the overturning moment about the same edge. Codes typically demand a ratio of at least 1.5 for permanent works, and 2.0 where consequences are severe or the loads uncertain. Take a free-standing masonry wall 2.5 metres tall, 0.4 metres thick, of density 2,000 kilograms per cubic metre, per metre of length. Its weight is 2.5 times 0.4 times 2,000 times 9.81, about 19.6 kilonewtons, acting 0.2 metres from the toe, giving a restoring moment of 3.92 kilonewton metres. A wind pressure of 0.6 kilopascals over the 2.5 metre height gives 1.5 kilonewtons acting at mid-height, 1.25 metres up, an overturning moment of 1.88 kilonewton metres. The ratio is 2.09, adequate. Raise the wall to 3.5 metres and the wind force rises to 2.1 kilonewtons at 1.75 metres, an overturning moment of 3.68, while the restoring moment rises only to 5.49, giving 1.49 — now marginal. Overturning penalises height far faster than it rewards weight.

Sliding is the companion check and must be done separately, comparing horizontal load against the available friction under the base. Many retaining walls that pass the overturning check fail the sliding one, especially on wet clay, which is why shear keys and toe projections are cast into their undersides.

sections.heading: Compression members and buckling
sections.body:
The most dangerous gap in a pure statics education is the belief that a member fails when its stress reaches the material strength. For members in tension that is broadly true. For slender members in compression it is badly false, and the difference has killed people. A long strut fails not by crushing but by buckling: at some critical load it suddenly bows sideways and loses all capacity, at a stress that may be a small fraction of the material's yield strength.

Leonhard Euler solved this in 1744. For a pin-ended column of length L, the critical buckling load equals pi squared times E times I divided by L squared, where E is Young's modulus and I is the second moment of area of the cross-section about its weakest axis. Three features of that formula deserve attention. First, the load depends on the square of length, so doubling a column's height cuts its buckling capacity to a quarter. Second, it depends on E, a stiffness property, not on strength at all: a high-strength steel column buckles at precisely the same load as a mild steel one of identical geometry, because their moduli are the same. Third, it depends on the weakest axis, so a column will always buckle about whichever direction has the smaller I, which is why a flat plank used as a prop is far weaker than its area suggests.

End conditions modify the effective length. A pinned-pinned column has an effective length equal to its true length. A column fixed at both ends has an effective length of about 0.5L, giving four times the capacity. Fixed at one end and free at the other — a flagpole or an unbraced cantilever prop — has an effective length of 2L, giving a quarter of the pinned capacity. Fixed-pinned is about 0.7L. Choosing and then actually achieving the assumed end condition on site is a recurring source of trouble, because a joint the designer treated as fixed is often, in the built reality, closer to pinned.

Slenderness ratio, defined as effective length divided by the radius of gyration of the section, decides which failure mode applies. Below roughly 30 for steel, the member simply squashes and material strength governs. Above about 120, Euler buckling governs almost entirely. Between those bounds sits an awkward intermediate region where a partly yielded, partly buckling failure occurs, handled in codes by empirical curves such as the Perry-Robertson formulation, which also account for the fact that no real column is perfectly straight or perfectly centrally loaded.

Initial crookedness matters enormously. A column with an initial bow of even span over 1,000, which is a normal manufacturing tolerance, has a measurably reduced capacity because the eccentricity generates bending from the very first increment of load. Buckling failure is also sudden and gives essentially no warning, in sharp contrast to a bending failure in ductile steel, which sags visibly first. That absence of warning is why compression members carry larger safety margins.

sections.heading: Loads: knowing what you are actually resisting
sections.body:
Equilibrium is only as good as the list of forces you put into it, and in real design the largest uncertainties live in the loads rather than the arithmetic. Loads are conventionally divided into permanent and variable. Permanent loads, sometimes called dead loads, are the self-weight of the structure and everything permanently attached: the slab, the screed, the finishes, the ceiling, the services. They are calculable to within a few per cent from densities and dimensions. Reinforced concrete is about 24 kilonewtons per cubic metre, structural steel about 78.5, softwood timber around 5, and brickwork roughly 18 to 22.

Variable loads, or live loads, are the transient ones: people, furniture, stored goods, vehicles, snow, wind. These are the domain of statistics rather than measurement, and codes specify characteristic values with a defined probability of exceedance. Typical figures give 1.5 kilopascals for domestic floors, 2.5 to 3.0 for offices and classrooms, 4.0 to 5.0 for assembly areas and shops, and 7.5 or more for heavy storage. A crowd packed shoulder to shoulder approaches 5 kilopascals, which is why assembly structures are designed so much more heavily than houses.

Wind is a pressure, and it grows with the square of speed. The dynamic pressure of moving air is approximately 0.613 times the square of velocity in metres per second, giving pascals. A 25 metre per second wind, about 90 kilometres per hour, produces roughly 383 pascals of dynamic pressure, which is then multiplied by shape factors that can exceed 1.0 for windward walls and produce suction on roofs and leeward faces. Suction on a lightweight roof is often the governing case, because uplift can exceed the roof's own weight and the fixings, not the rafters, become the critical element.

Snow accumulates unevenly and is heavier than intuition suggests: fresh snow is around 1 kilonewton per cubic metre, but settled and wet it reaches 3 or 4. Drift against a parapet or in a valley gutter can double or triple the uniform value locally, and roof collapses under snow almost always trace to drifting rather than to the average depth. Water is worse, because ponding is self-reinforcing: a flat roof deflects, water pools in the dip, the extra weight deepens the dip, and more water arrives.

Because loads are uncertain, modern codes apply partial safety factors rather than one global factor. A common European arrangement multiplies permanent loads by 1.35 and variable loads by 1.5, then divides material strengths by factors of 1.0 to 1.5 depending on the material's variability, with concrete penalised more than steel. Combination rules also prevent absurd accumulations, since maximum wind and maximum crowd and maximum snow will not plausibly coincide. The philosophy is honest: uncertainty is quantified where it lives, rather than concealed in a single number.

sections.heading: Failure modes, limits, and what to do when it goes wrong
sections.body:
Statics assumes nothing accelerates, and where that assumption breaks the answers can be badly wrong. A load applied suddenly rather than gradually produces up to twice the deflection and internal force of the same load placed gently. A load arriving repeatedly at the structure's own natural frequency produces far more, because resonance accumulates energy cycle after cycle. The Tacoma Narrows bridge tore itself apart on 7 November 1940 in a wind of only about 19 metres per second, through an aeroelastic flutter no static pressure calculation could have predicted. Time causes a second departure: concrete creeps under sustained load, with long-term deflection two or three times the immediate elastic value, while steel fatigues, repeated cycles far below yield propagating a crack to failure.

The failure modes worth naming are few, and identifying which one is developing tells you how much warning you have. Bending failure in a ductile material sags visibly and gives generous notice. Shear failure, especially near supports, arrives as a diagonal crack and is abrupt. Buckling is sudden and essentially without warning. Connection failure — a bolt group tearing out, a weld cracking, a joist hanger pulling free — is by a wide margin the most common real cause, because connections concentrate force into small areas and are the part most often altered or damaged on site. Foundation failure shows as cracks wider at one end and doors that stop closing.

The honest limit of the subject is that statics answers whether forces balance, not whether a structure is safe. Safety also requires the load estimate, the material capacity, the connection detail, the workmanship and the possibility of misuse. And no amount of analysis rescues a structure built differently from the drawing.
steps: Stop loading it and get people clear. Most collapses are preceded by minutes to days of visible warning, and the cheapest intervention is to remove the load and the occupants first, then investigate.
Trace the load path from where force is applied, through each member, to the ground. Any point where you cannot name the next element in the chain is where the problem probably lies.
Draw a free body diagram of the suspect element in isolation, marking every force from every object touching it, including its own weight at its centre of gravity.
Balance vertical forces, horizontal forces and moments, taking moments about the most inconvenient unknown so that it drops out of the equation.
Convert internal force to stress by dividing by the resisting area, or for bending by dividing moment by section modulus, then compare against a conservative material capacity.
Check what equilibrium does not reveal: buckling of every compression member about its weakest axis, sliding and overturning of the whole assembly, and the capacity of each connection.
Prop conservatively. A temporary prop must itself be checked for buckling, must bear on something that carries load down to firm ground, and must be restrained so it cannot be knocked out.
Have a qualified engineer inspect anything permanent, load-bearing or occupied. A hand calculation identifies a problem; it does not license a repair.

guides.title: Strength of materials: stress, strain and deformation
guides.summary: How solid materials respond to load: the definitions of stress and strain, elastic and plastic behaviour, bending, torsion, buckling and fatigue, and the failure theories engineers use to decide whether a part is safe. Closes with how to read a broken component and what to do about a structure in distress.

sections.heading: Why a separate science of material strength exists
sections.body:
Statics tells you the forces acting on a structure; it says nothing about whether the structure survives them. A roof truss carrying 40 kilonewtons at a joint is in perfect equilibrium whether the members are steel tubes or drinking straws. The discipline that closes that gap is called strength of materials, or mechanics of materials, and its central question is deceptively simple: given a body of known shape made of a known material, and given the loads applied to it, will it break, will it bend too far to be useful, and how much will it move? Everything else in the subject is machinery built to answer those three questions.

The historical starting point is usually placed with Galileo Galilei, whose 1638 Discourses examined a stone cantilever projecting from a wall and asked how its breaking load scaled with its dimensions.
