He got the answer partly wrong, because he assumed the whole cross-section pulled uniformly, but he asked the right question and established the crucial scaling insight that strength grows with area while weight grows with volume. That single observation explains why a mouse can fall down a mineshaft and walk away, why an insect's legs look absurdly thin, and why you cannot simply photograph a small bridge and build it ten times larger. Robert Hooke published his law of elasticity in 1678 as the anagram ceiiinosssttuv, unscrambling to ut tensio sic vis, "as the extension, so the force." Thomas Young gave the modern stiffness constant its meaning around 1807. Augustin-Louis Cauchy formalised stress as a tensor quantity in the 1820s, and by the mid-nineteenth century the framework used in practice today was essentially complete.

The subject sits between two neighbours and it helps to know the borders. Rigid-body statics treats every object as undeformable and asks only about equilibrium. The theory of elasticity treats the full three-dimensional continuum with partial differential equations and is exact but intractable by hand for most real shapes. Strength of materials occupies the pragmatic middle: it accepts a few simplifying assumptions about how sections deform, and in exchange it produces closed-form formulas that a person can evaluate with a pencil and check against intuition. Knowing where those simplifications break down is a large part of competence in the field.

The reason this matters outside a classroom is that the failures are not gradual and forgiving. A ductile steel beam gives warning: it sags, it groans, the paint flakes along the tension face. A cast iron beam, a weld with a hidden crack, or a bolt loaded beyond its proof stress can go from apparently fine to completely severed in milliseconds with no warning at all. Understanding which regime you are in, and therefore whether the structure will warn you before it lets go, is arguably the single most useful thing this subject teaches. It also teaches humility about numbers. Real materials vary batch to batch, real loads exceed the nominal figures, real geometry has scratches and holes and corners, and the honest engineer builds in margin rather than pretending the calculation is exact.

sections.heading: Stress: force intensity, not force
sections.body:
Stress is the intensity of internal force, defined as force divided by the area over which it acts. Its symbol is usually the Greek sigma for normal stress and tau for shear stress, and its unit in the metric system is the pascal, one newton per square metre. A pascal is tiny — roughly the pressure of a sheet of paper resting on a table — so engineering work is done in megapascals (MPa, one million pascals, equal to one newton per square millimetre) or gigapascals (GPa, one thousand MPa). In United States practice the unit is pounds per square inch, psi, or thousands of pounds per square inch, ksi. The conversion worth memorising is that 1 ksi is about 6.895 MPa, so a 36 ksi mild steel yield is close to 250 MPa.

The distinction between stress and force is not pedantry, it is the whole point. A 10 kilonewton pull applied to a 100 square millimetre bar produces 100 MPa. The same pull applied to a 10 square millimetre bar produces 1000 MPa and will destroy most steels. The force has not changed; only its concentration has. This is why a thumbtack works, why a sharp knife cuts and a blunt one does not, and why snowshoes keep you on the surface. It is also why the single most common cause of unexpected structural failure is a reduction in area that nobody accounted for: a bolt hole, a keyway, a corrosion pit, a weld undercut.

Normal stress acts perpendicular to a surface and is called tensile when it pulls the material apart and compressive when it pushes it together. Sign convention almost universally makes tension positive. Shear stress acts parallel to the surface, sliding one layer across another; it is what a rivet feels when the plates it joins try to slide past each other, and what a bolt in a lap joint carries. In a real loaded body, the stress at a point is not a single number. It is a nine-component tensor, reducing by symmetry to six independent values: three normal stresses on three mutually perpendicular planes, and three shear stresses. Cauchy's insight was that if you know the stress on three perpendicular planes at a point, you can compute the stress on any plane through that point.

That has an important practical consequence. Because the stress on a plane depends on the plane's orientation, every point in a loaded body has particular orientations where the shear stress vanishes entirely and the normal stress reaches its maximum and minimum values. These are the principal stresses, and they matter because most failure criteria are expressed in terms of them. A bar in pure tension at 100 MPa is also, on planes at 45 degrees to its axis, carrying 50 MPa of shear — which is exactly why ductile metals pulled in tension shear off along a cone at roughly 45 degrees rather than parting cleanly across the section.

sections.heading: Strain: measuring deformation without units
sections.body:
Strain is the geometric response to stress: the deformation of a body expressed as a fraction of its original dimension. For a bar of original length L stretched by an amount delta, the normal strain epsilon is delta divided by L. Because it is a length divided by a length, strain is dimensionless. Engineering quantities are typically small, so strain is quoted as a percentage, or in microstrain, where one microstrain equals one part per million, or 0.000001. A structural steel member at working load might be at 500 to 700 microstrain; the same steel yields around 1200 microstrain and can stretch beyond 200000 microstrain, that is 20 percent, before it finally tears.

Shear strain, symbol gamma, is the angular distortion of an originally right angle, measured in radians. Push the top of a rubber block sideways so that a face originally at 90 degrees now sits at 89 degrees and the shear strain is one degree converted to radians, about 0.0175. A useful mental picture is that normal strain changes a body's size while shear strain changes its shape.

There is a subtlety that becomes important at large deformations. Engineering strain divides the change in length by the ORIGINAL length, which is convenient but progressively inaccurate as the specimen stretches, because the material is no longer the length you divided by. True strain integrates the incremental change against the instantaneous length, giving the natural logarithm of final length over initial length. At one percent strain the two definitions differ by half a percent and nobody cares. At 50 percent strain, engineering strain reads 0.50 while true strain reads 0.405, and the difference is decisive. Metal forming, deep drawing and crash analysis use true measures; ordinary structural design lives comfortably in the engineering definition.

Strain is measured in practice with a bonded electrical resistance strain gauge, a foil grid glued to the surface whose resistance changes as it stretches. The gauge factor, typically about 2.0 for constantan foil, relates fractional resistance change to strain; a Wheatstone bridge circuit converts that into a voltage. Because the change is minute — 1000 microstrain shifts a 350 ohm gauge by about 0.7 ohms — bridge completion, temperature compensation and lead-wire resistance all matter enormously, and a careless installation reads temperature far more faithfully than load. Optical methods now compete strongly: digital image correlation photographs a speckle pattern before and after loading and computes a full-field strain map by tracking the pattern, which reveals strain concentrations a discrete gauge would miss entirely. For quick field diagnosis, brittle lacquer coatings and even a thin layer of whitewash on rusty steel will crack along lines of high tensile strain and show you where a structure is actually working hardest.

sections.heading: Hooke's law, Young's modulus and the elastic constants
sections.body:
For small deformations most engineering solids obey a linear relation between stress and strain: sigma equals E times epsilon. The constant E is Young's modulus, also called the modulus of elasticity, and it is the material's stiffness — the stress required to produce unit strain. Because strain is dimensionless, E carries the units of stress, and for metals it is large. Structural steel sits at about 200 GPa regardless of grade, which is a fact of enormous practical importance: a mild steel and a high-strength alloy steel bend by exactly the same amount under the same load, they simply differ in when they stop coming back. Aluminium alloys are near 69 GPa, roughly one third of steel. Titanium is about 110 GPa, copper 117, cast iron 100 to 170 depending on graphite form, concrete 20 to 40, softwood along the grain 8 to 14, and most rigid plastics between 1 and 4 GPa. Diamond, at about 1050 GPa, is the stiffest bulk material commonly cited, though carbon nanotubes measured along their axis are stiffer still.

Stiffness and strength are independent properties and confusing them causes real design errors. A glass fibre and a steel rod may fail at similar stresses, but the glass fibre stretches several times further first. Rubber has a modulus around 0.01 GPa yet can be extremely tough. If a floor feels bouncy, the problem is stiffness and a stronger steel will not help; you need more depth, which enters the deflection formula as a cube or a fourth power.

Pull a bar longitudinally and it gets thinner transversely. The ratio of transverse contraction strain to longitudinal extension strain, taken positive, is Poisson's ratio, symbol nu, named for Siméon Poisson who derived it around 1829. Most metals are near 0.3, cork close to 0.0, which is precisely why a cork can be pushed into a bottleneck without bulging, and rubber approaches 0.5, the theoretical limit for an incompressible solid. A handful of engineered foams and lattice structures are auxetic, with negative Poisson's ratio, getting fatter when stretched.

For an isotropic material — one whose properties are the same in every direction — only two independent elastic constants exist, and every other constant follows. The shear modulus G equals E divided by twice the quantity one plus nu, which for steel gives about 77 GPa. The bulk modulus K, relating hydrostatic pressure to volumetric strain, equals E divided by three times the quantity one minus two nu. That last expression explains the incompressibility limit: as nu approaches 0.5 the denominator vanishes and K goes to infinity.

Not all materials are isotropic. Wood is dramatically stronger and stiffer along the grain than across it, often by a factor of twenty in tension. Rolled sheet metal, forged parts and fibre composites are all directional. A carbon fibre laminate can be designed with a modulus of 130 GPa in the fibre direction and 9 GPa transverse in the same sheet, which is a feature rather than a defect if the designer aligns the fibres with the load path and a catastrophe if they do not.

sections.heading: Reading a stress-strain curve
sections.body:
The tensile test is the foundational experiment of the subject. A machined specimen with a reduced central gauge section is gripped in a testing machine and pulled at a controlled rate while load and extension are recorded. Dividing load by original area and extension by original gauge length yields the engineering stress-strain curve, and almost everything a designer needs to know about a metal can be read off it.

The curve begins as a straight line whose slope is Young's modulus. It stays straight up to the proportional limit. Slightly beyond that lies the elastic limit, the largest stress from which the specimen still returns exactly to its original length on unloading. In practice these two are hard to distinguish experimentally, so engineers use a defined offset yield strength: draw a line parallel to the elastic slope but displaced 0.2 percent along the strain axis, and where it intersects the curve is the 0.2 percent proof stress, written Rp0.2. This is the number that appears on material certificates and in design codes. Low-carbon steels are unusual in showing a genuine yield point, where load actually drops as dislocations tear free of carbon atmospheres, producing an upper and lower yield point and the visible Lüders bands that streak across a bent mild steel sheet.

Past yield the material work-hardens: dislocations multiply and tangle, so further deformation requires more stress and the curve climbs again, though far more shallowly. It peaks at the ultimate tensile strength, UTS. For structural steel S275, yield is 275 MPa and UTS about 430 MPa. For S355, 355 and roughly 490. A 6061-T6 aluminium is near 275 yield and 310 UTS. A quenched and tempered alloy steel like 4340 can exceed 1500 MPa.

After the peak, deformation localises. One region thins faster than the rest, its area falls, the true stress there rises sharply, and the process runs away — this is necking. The engineering curve falls after the UTS not because the material weakens but because the plotted stress is still being divided by the original area while the real area is shrinking. Fracture follows, and in a ductile metal it shows the classic cup-and-cone surface: a fibrous centre where microvoids around inclusions grow and coalesce, surrounded by a shear lip at about 45 degrees.

Two ductility measures come from the broken specimen. Percentage elongation is the permanent stretch of the gauge length, typically 20 to 25 percent for structural steel and often under 5 percent for a hardened tool steel. Percentage reduction of area at the neck is the more sensitive measure. The area under the whole curve up to fracture is toughness, the energy per unit volume absorbed, and the area under the elastic portion alone is resilience, the energy stored and returned — the property that matters for a spring. A material can be very strong yet not tough at all: glass, ceramics, and hardened steel all fail this way.

sections.heading: Elastic, plastic and time-dependent behaviour
sections.body:
Elastic deformation is reversible. The atoms stretch apart against their interatomic bonds and spring back when released, which is why the elastic modulus correlates strongly with melting point and bond strength and why it changes only slowly with heat treatment. You cannot make steel meaningfully stiffer by alloying or quenching, only stronger. Plastic deformation is permanent. In crystalline metals it happens by dislocation glide: line defects in the crystal lattice sweep through, shifting one plane of atoms by one atomic spacing at a time, in the same way a rucked carpet is moved by pushing a wrinkle across it rather than dragging the whole sheet. Because the wrinkle costs far less force than the sheet, real metals yield at stresses perhaps a thousand times lower than the theoretical strength of a perfect crystal.

Everything metallurgists do to strengthen a metal is an attempt to obstruct dislocations. Cold working multiplies them until they jam each other. Alloying puts foreign atoms in the lattice that strain it and impede glide. Precipitation hardening, as in 6061-T6 aluminium or 17-4 stainless, grows fine second-phase particles that dislocations must cut or bow around. Grain refinement adds boundaries that dislocations cannot cross, described by the Hall-Petch relation in which yield strength rises with the inverse square root of grain diameter. Quenching steel traps carbon in a distorted martensitic lattice. Every one of these mechanisms raises strength and, almost without exception, lowers ductility and toughness. That trade-off is the central bargain of metallurgy.

Time enters in two important ways. Creep is slow continuous deformation under constant load, significant when the absolute temperature exceeds roughly 0.3 to 0.4 of the melting temperature. For steel that means above about 370 degrees Celsius, which is why boiler and turbine design uses creep-rupture data rather than room-temperature yield, and why fire is so destructive to steel frames: at 550 degrees Celsius structural steel retains only about 60 percent of its room-temperature yield strength, and near 700 degrees only about 20 percent. Lead and solder creep at room temperature, which is why old lead roofing sags and why a soldered joint should never be the sole mechanical support. Polymers creep badly; a plastic shelf loaded for a year takes a permanent set.

Viscoelasticity is the related behaviour in which the response depends on rate. Pull a polymer slowly and it flows; strike it fast and it behaves like a brittle glass. Stress relaxation is the same phenomenon seen at constant strain: a tightened bolt in a hot flange loses preload over months without anything moving. Silly putty is the classroom demonstration, bouncing when thrown and puddling when left. Where relaxation matters, designers specify a higher initial preload, use disc springs to store elastic reserve, or schedule retorquing.

sections.heading: Axial members, thermal stress and statical indeterminacy
sections.body:
The simplest structural element is a bar carrying load along its axis. Its stress is force divided by cross-sectional area, its strain is stress divided by Young's modulus, and its extension is force times length divided by the product of area and modulus, written delta equals PL over AE. The quantity AE over L is the bar's axial stiffness in newtons per millimetre, and it behaves exactly like a spring constant, which means bars in parallel add their stiffnesses while bars in series add their flexibilities. A worked case: a 3 metre steel tie rod of 20 millimetre diameter carries 60 kilonewtons. Its area is 314 square millimetres, so the stress is 191 MPa, comfortably under a 275 MPa yield. Its extension is 60000 times 3000 divided by 314 times 200000, which is 2.9 millimetres. Whether that is acceptable is a serviceability question quite separate from strength.

Temperature change produces strain without stress if the member is free to move. The free thermal strain is the coefficient of linear expansion alpha multiplied by the temperature change. Steel is about 12 microstrain per degree Celsius, aluminium 23, copper 17, concrete conveniently close to steel at 10 to 12 — the coincidence that makes reinforced concrete possible at all — and ordinary glass about 9, while borosilicate is 3.3, which is why Pyrex survives thermal shock that shatters soda-lime glass. If the member is restrained, the strain it wanted to have is converted into stress: sigma equals E times alpha times delta T. For steel, that is 200000 times 0.000012, or 2.4 MPa for every degree. A 40 degree summer swing on a fully restrained steel member generates 96 MPa out of nothing. This is why bridges have expansion joints, why long pipe runs contain expansion loops or bellows, why rails are laid with a stress-free temperature and welded track can buckle in heatwaves, and why a mismatch of expansion coefficients across a bonded joint tears it apart on thermal cycling.

Many real assemblies are statically indeterminate, meaning equilibrium equations alone cannot find the internal forces. A rigid plate supported by three columns of different length, a bolted flange, a composite bar of steel sleeved in brass — in each case there are more unknowns than equations. The resolution is always the same three-step method and it is worth internalising because it generalises to every branch of the subject. First write equilibrium. Second write compatibility, a geometric statement of how the deformations must relate, for instance that two members bonded together must stretch equally. Third substitute the force-deformation relation for each member into the compatibility equation. The result is that load distributes in proportion to stiffness. In a steel-and-brass composite column, the steel takes roughly twice the stress of the brass because its modulus is roughly twice as large. That principle — load follows stiffness — is one of the most useful heuristics in engineering, and it explains why adding a stiff element to a structure attracts load to it rather than simply sharing the burden evenly.

sections.heading: Bending: the beam formula and second moment of area
sections.body:
A beam loaded transversely does not carry that load by stretching; it carries it by developing an internal bending moment, and the way it does so is the most consequential idea in structural engineering. Consider a beam sagging under load. Its top fibres shorten, its bottom fibres lengthen, and somewhere in between lies a surface that does neither — the neutral axis, which for an elastic homogeneous section passes through the centroid. The Euler-Bernoulli assumption is that plane sections remain plane and perpendicular to the neutral axis, from which strain must vary linearly with distance y from that axis. With Hooke's law, stress does the same, giving the flexure formula: sigma equals M times y divided by I, where M is the bending moment and I is the second moment of area.

I is a purely geometric property with units of length to the fourth power, and it measures how far the material is placed from the neutral axis. For a rectangle of width b and depth d bent about its horizontal axis, I equals b times d cubed divided by twelve. The cube is the crucial term. Doubling a joist's width doubles its bending stiffness; doubling its depth multiplies it by eight. This is why floor joists stand on edge, why a flat sheet of paper flops while the same sheet curved into a channel supports itself, and why corrugating thin metal roofing transforms it. For a solid circular shaft, I is pi times diameter to the fourth over 64.

Because stress is greatest at the extreme fibre, designers use the section modulus Z, defined as I divided by the maximum y, so that peak stress is simply M over Z. Efficient sections push area to the extremes and leave only enough material in the middle to carry shear and hold the flanges apart — hence the universal I-beam, in which perhaps 85 percent of the bending resistance lives in the flanges. A 203 by 133 UB25 section has a Z near 230000 cubic millimetres, so at 275 MPa it resists about 63 kilonewton-metres of moment — several times what a solid square bar of equal weight could manage.

Bending also produces transverse shear, distributed across the depth by the relation tau equals VQ over It, where V is the shear force, Q is the first moment of the area beyond the level of interest, and t is the width there. For a rectangle, shear stress is zero at the surfaces and peaks at the neutral axis at 1.5 times the average. In an I-beam almost all the shear is carried by the web. This is why a short deep beam can fail in shear rather than bending, and why notches cut in a joist — the exact place a plumber likes to run a pipe — are so much more damaging than they look. The safe rule for timber joists is to notch only in the outer third of the span, no deeper than one eighth of the depth, and to drill holes only near the neutral axis.

sections.heading: Deflection, stiffness and serviceability
sections.body:
Strength answers whether a member breaks. Deflection answers whether it is usable, and in modern design with high-strength materials the deflection limit governs far more often than the stress limit. The governing relation comes from the curvature of the elastic line: the second derivative of deflection with respect to position equals the bending moment divided by EI. Integrating twice with the appropriate boundary conditions gives the deflected shape, and standard results are tabulated for every common case.

The three worth committing to memory cover most situations. A simply supported beam with a uniformly distributed load w over span L deflects at midspan by 5wL to the fourth divided by 384EI. The same beam with a central point load P deflects by PL cubed over 48EI. A cantilever of length L with a point load at the tip deflects by PL cubed over 3EI. Notice the powers. Deflection goes as span to the third or fourth power, so doubling a span multiplies deflection by eight or sixteen. It is inversely proportional to E and to I, and since I for a rectangle contains depth cubed, deflection scales as one over depth cubed. If a floor bounces, adding depth is overwhelmingly the most effective fix, followed by reducing span with an intermediate support; changing to a stronger grade of the same material accomplishes nothing at all, because E is essentially constant across grades.

Serviceability limits are conventional rather than physical. Building codes commonly restrict deflection under imposed load to span divided by 360 for plastered ceilings, span over 250 for general cases, and span over 200 for roofs without brittle finishes. A 4 metre floor joist at L over 360 is therefore allowed 11 millimetres. These figures exist because plaster cracks, doors jam, tiles debond, and occupants become alarmed long before anything is structurally at risk. Vibration is a separate criterion, and long-span lightweight floors can satisfy every deflection rule while still feeling unpleasantly lively; a common target is a fundamental frequency above 8 hertz.

Two practical techniques follow from the mathematics. Precambering builds a deliberate upward curvature into a beam or truss so that under dead load it settles flat, a standard practice in long-span steel and in glulam. Superposition allows the deflections and moments from several separate load cases to be added, valid as long as the material stays linear elastic and displacements remain small. The moment-area theorems and Macaulay's step-function method are the classical hand tools for irregular loading, and both remain useful for sanity-checking computer output. That check matters: a finite element model with a mis-specified support condition will return a beautifully rendered and completely wrong deflection, and the standard table result is often the only thing that catches it.

sections.heading: Torsion, shafts and thin-walled sections
sections.body:
Twisting a circular shaft produces pure shear. The governing relation, the torsion formula, states that shear stress tau equals torque T times radial distance r divided by the polar second moment of area J, and that the angle of twist in radians equals TL divided by GJ, where G is the shear modulus. For a solid circular shaft J equals pi times diameter to the fourth divided by 32; for a hollow shaft it is pi times the outer diameter to the fourth minus the inner to the fourth, again over 32. Stress is zero at the centre and maximum at the surface, which means the core of a solid shaft contributes weight and almost no strength. Removing the inner 50 percent of the diameter costs only about six percent of the torsional capacity while saving a quarter of the mass, and this is precisely why drive shafts, bicycle axles and aircraft structures are hollow.

A worked example fixes the scale. A 40 millimetre solid steel shaft transmitting 15 kilowatts at 1500 revolutions per minute carries a torque of power divided by angular velocity: 15000 divided by 157 radians per second gives 95.5 newton-metres. J is pi times 40 to the fourth over 32, about 251000 millimetres to the fourth, so the surface shear stress is 95500 times 20 divided by 251000, roughly 7.6 MPa. That is trivially low, which tells you immediately that such a shaft is sized by bearing loads, keyway stress concentration or critical speed rather than by torsional strength — a very common situation in machine design.

Non-circular sections behave quite differently and the simple formula does not apply. A rectangular bar in torsion warps: plane sections do not remain plane, corners carry no shear at all, and the maximum stress occurs at the midpoint of the longer side. Empirical coefficients from Saint-Venant's analysis are used instead. More important is the vast difference between closed and open thin-walled sections. A closed tube resists torque by a continuous shear flow around its perimeter, described by Bredt's formula in which shear flow equals torque divided by twice the enclosed area. Slit that tube lengthwise and its torsional stiffness collapses by two or three orders of magnitude, because the only remaining mechanism is a small circulating shear within each wall thickness. A 100 millimetre square tube may be several thousand times stiffer in torsion than the same tube with a hairline slot cut along its length. This single fact explains why open channel and I sections twist so readily, why they need torsional restraint at supports, why aircraft wings are built as closed torsion boxes, and why cutting an access hole in a closed structural member without reinforcing it is one of the more expensive mistakes an amateur can make.

Combined bending and torsion is the normal condition for a real shaft, and it is handled by computing an equivalent bending moment or by taking the stresses to a failure criterion, which for ductile shafts is usually the maximum shear stress or distortion energy theory applied at the surface where both stresses peak.

sections.heading: Columns, buckling and instability
sections.body:
A short compression member fails by crushing when the stress reaches yield. A long one fails at a fraction of that load by suddenly bowing sideways, and the transition between these regimes is one of the sharpest discontinuities in structural behaviour. Buckling is not a strength failure at all; it is an instability, a point at which the straight configuration ceases to be the energetically preferred one, and it can occur while the material is still entirely elastic and undamaged.

Leonhard Euler solved the elastic case in 1757. The critical load equals pi squared times EI divided by the effective length squared. Three things follow. First, material strength does not appear — a high-strength steel column buckles at exactly the same load as a mild steel one of identical geometry, which is among the most counterintuitive and most frequently forgotten results in the subject. Second, the relevant I is the smallest one, about the weak axis, because the column will find its easiest escape route. Third, effective length depends on end restraint: a pin-ended column has effective length equal to its actual length; a column fixed at both ends has an effective length of 0.5L and therefore four times the capacity; fixed at one end and free at the other, as in a flagpole or a cantilevered sign post, the effective length is 2L and capacity drops to one quarter. Fixed-pinned gives about 0.7L. These factors are worth memorising because improving end fixity is often far cheaper than increasing section size.

The Euler curve is plotted against slenderness ratio, effective length divided by radius of gyration, where the radius of gyration is the square root of I over A. Below a slenderness of roughly 90 to 100 for structural steel, the Euler prediction exceeds the squash load and is meaningless; real columns in this intermediate range fail by inelastic buckling, and codes use empirical curves — Perry-Robertson, Johnson parabolic, or the tabulated buckling curves of Eurocode 3 — that account for initial crookedness, residual stresses from rolling or welding, and accidental load eccentricity. Real columns are never perfectly straight, and an initial bow of L over 1000 is a typical manufacturing tolerance that measurably reduces capacity.

Buckling has many relatives. Lateral-torsional buckling afflicts deep slender beams, which roll sideways and twist out from under their load unless the compression flange is restrained — the reason a joist needs blocking or a nailed deck. Local buckling wrinkles a thin flange or web before the whole member does anything, governed by the width-to-thickness ratio and the reason sections are classified as plastic, compact, semi-compact or slender. Shells buckle notoriously unpredictably, with real cylinders often reaching only 20 to 30 percent of the classical theoretical load because of imperfection sensitivity; a thin-walled drinks can supports a person until a tiny dent triggers instant collapse. Snap-through buckling reverses a shallow arch or dome abruptly. In every case the warning signs are the same: slenderness, thinness, compression, and inadequate restraint.

sections.heading: Combined stresses, Mohr's circle and failure theories
sections.body:
Real components rarely see one kind of stress alone. A pressure vessel nozzle carries hoop tension, longitudinal tension, bending from an attached pipe and thermal stress simultaneously. To decide whether such a state is safe, the several stresses must be reduced to a single number that can be compared to a material property from a simple tensile test. That reduction is what a failure theory does.

The first step is finding the principal stresses. For the common plane-stress case with normal stresses sigma-x and sigma-y and shear tau, the two principal values are the average of sigma-x and sigma-y, plus and minus the square root of the quantity half the difference squared plus tau squared. The maximum in-plane shear stress equals that square-root term. Otto Mohr's graphical construction of 1882 plots this as a circle centred on the average stress with radius equal to the maximum shear, and though software has replaced the drafting, the circle remains the clearest way to see that rotating the plane trades normal stress for shear and that principal planes are always 45 degrees from planes of maximum shear.

For ductile metals two criteria dominate. The maximum shear stress theory, due to Tresca in the 1860s, holds that yielding begins when the maximum shear stress reaches the value it had at yield in a tensile test, namely half the yield strength. Expressed in principal stresses, failure occurs when the largest principal stress minus the smallest reaches the yield strength. The distortion energy theory, developed by Maxwell, Huber, von Mises and Hencky, holds that yielding depends only on the energy of shape change and not of volume change; it produces the von Mises equivalent stress, and it matches experimental data on metals better than Tresca, typically within a few percent. Tresca is always the more conservative of the two, by up to 15 percent, and remains popular in pressure vessel codes for that reason. Both predict that pure hydrostatic pressure, however enormous, never causes yielding — a prediction confirmed by experiments in which metals compressed under thousands of atmospheres of uniform pressure show no permanent deformation whatsoever.

Brittle materials need different criteria because they fail by crack propagation from tensile stress rather than by dislocation motion. Maximum normal stress theory, sometimes called Rankine's, simply compares the largest principal tensile stress to the tensile strength. For materials far stronger in compression than tension — grey cast iron at perhaps 200 MPa tension and 800 MPa compression, concrete at a ratio near ten to one, rock and masonry similarly — the Mohr-Coulomb criterion interpolates between the two strengths and predicts the characteristic failure angles seen in a crushed concrete cylinder. This asymmetry governs entire building traditions: masonry arches, vaults and domes exist because stone is superb in compression and nearly useless in tension, and the whole art is shaping the structure so the line of thrust stays inside the material.

sections.heading: Stress concentration and the geometry of trouble
sections.body:
The flexure and axial formulas assume smooth, uniform geometry. Real parts have holes, fillets, keyways, threads, grooves, weld toes and tool marks, and at every such feature the stress lines crowd together and the local stress rises far above the nominal value. The multiplier is the stress concentration factor Kt, defined as peak local stress divided by nominal stress computed on the net section, and it is purely geometric — it does not depend on the material or on the load magnitude.

The canonical case is a small circular hole in a wide plate under uniform tension, for which the theoretical elasticity solution, published by Kirsch in 1898, gives exactly 3.0 at the hole edge. An elliptical hole with its long axis across the load is far worse: Kt equals one plus twice the ratio of the semi-axis perpendicular to the load over the one parallel to it, so a crack-like slot approaches infinity. A sharp reentrant corner is mathematically singular. This is why a square hatch in a ship or aircraft must have generously rounded corners, and why the loss of the Comet airliners in 1954 was traced to fatigue cracking from the corners of near-square cabin windows and inspection cutouts. A shoulder fillet on a shaft typically gives Kt between 1.5 and 3 depending on the ratio of fillet radius to shaft diameter, and the practical rule is simple and powerful: the bigger the radius, the lower the concentration. Doubling a fillet radius from 0.5 millimetres to 2 millimetres on a 25 millimetre shaft can drop Kt from about 2.5 to about 1.6, which in fatigue terms may triple the life for zero material cost.

Ductile materials under static load are forgiving of concentrations because the peak simply yields, redistributes and blunts itself — the plastic zone acts as a pressure-relief valve, so static design usually ignores Kt for ductile metals. Nothing else is forgiving. Under cyclic loading the concentration governs directly, moderated by a notch sensitivity factor. Brittle materials feel the full factor immediately, which is how a glass cutter works: the score line is a controlled stress raiser, and the sheet parts along it under trivial bending. Composites, ceramics and hardened steels must all be designed as if the concentration were fully effective.

Countermeasures are largely geometric. Increase radii everywhere. Add relief grooves alongside a shoulder to soften the transition. Drill a stop hole at the tip of a crack to convert a singular point into a modest circular concentration and buy time. Dress weld toes by grinding. Introduce compressive residual stress at the surface by shot peening, roller burnishing, cold expansion of fastener holes or carburising, all of which subtract from any applied tension at the very location where a crack would start. Aircraft fastener holes are routinely cold-expanded with a tapered mandrel for exactly this reason. Finally, respect the surface. A rough machined finish at 6.3 micrometres Ra can cut the fatigue limit of a high-strength steel by 20 to 30 percent relative to a polished one, and a scratch from a careless spanner is a manufactured crack starter.

sections.heading: Fatigue: failure under repeated load
sections.body:
Most machinery that breaks in service does not break because someone overloaded it once. It breaks because a stress far below yield was applied and removed several million times. Fatigue accounts for the majority of mechanical failures in service — figures of 80 to 90 percent are commonly quoted — and it is insidious precisely because the part looks perfectly fine right up to the moment it separates.

The mechanism runs in three stages. Initiation occurs at a surface discontinuity where cyclic plastic strain in a few grains extrudes and intrudes material until a microcrack forms. Propagation follows, the crack advancing a small increment on each cycle and leaving behind a smooth, often shell-like surface marked with beach marks that record changes in loading. Final fracture happens abruptly when the remaining ligament can no longer carry the peak load. A fatigue fracture surface is therefore diagnostic and readable without instruments: a smooth burnished region with curved arrest lines converging on an origin, adjoining a rough crystalline or fibrous region. If you find that pattern on a broken shaft, the answer is fatigue and the origin will point at the geometric feature responsible.

Design data comes from the S-N curve, plotting stress amplitude against cycles to failure on logarithmic axes, developed by August Wöhler in the 1860s after investigating railway axle failures. Ferrous metals and titanium characteristically show an endurance limit, a stress below which life appears indefinite, at roughly 40 to 50 percent of the ultimate tensile strength for wrought steels, and conventionally established at ten million cycles. Aluminium, copper and most non-ferrous alloys show no true endurance limit; their curves keep descending, so a fatigue strength must be quoted at a stated life such as 500 million cycles. This distinction has real consequences — an aluminium bicycle frame or aircraft component has a finite life by nature, whatever the stress, and must be inspected or retired accordingly.

Several factors modify the laboratory endurance limit and Marin's correction factors formalise them: surface finish, size (larger parts are weaker because more volume means more chances of a defect), type of loading (axial loading is worse than bending), temperature, and reliability. Mean stress matters greatly. A tensile mean stress opens cracks and reduces allowable amplitude; the Goodman and Gerber relations describe the trade-off, drawing a line from the fully reversed endurance limit on the amplitude axis to the ultimate strength on the mean axis. Compressive mean stress is beneficial, the physical basis for shot peening. Variable-amplitude loading is handled approximately by Miner's rule, summing the fractions of life consumed at each stress level and predicting failure when the sum reaches one, an assumption known to be crude — real damage sums at failure scatter between about 0.3 and 3 — but still the standard first estimate. Corrosion combined with cycling is worse than the sum of its parts and destroys the endurance limit entirely.

sections.heading: Fracture mechanics, brittleness and temperature
sections.body:
Classical strength of materials assumes a flawless body. Fracture mechanics assumes the opposite — that every real component contains cracks, and asks how large a crack a given material can tolerate at a given stress. The discipline began with A. A. Griffith's 1920 work on glass, which explained why bulk glass fails at perhaps 50 MPa when its theoretical strength is above 10000 MPa: energy released by crack growth exceeds the energy needed to create new surface once the crack exceeds a critical length. George Irwin extended it to metals in the 1950s, adding the plastic work at the crack tip and defining the stress intensity factor K, which equals a geometry factor times the applied stress times the square root of pi times crack length.

Failure occurs when K reaches a material property called the fracture toughness, KIC, measured in MPa times the square root of a metre. Typical values span an enormous range: glass and ceramics 0.7 to 5, cast iron around 6 to 20, a very high-strength maraging steel 40 to 90, structural steel 50 to 150 or more, aluminium alloys 20 to 45, and tough pressure-vessel steels above 200. The practical inversion of the formula gives critical crack length, and it produces sobering numbers. A steel with KIC of 50 MPa root-metre stressed at 300 MPa tolerates a through-crack of about 8.8 millimetres half-length. Raise the strength and the toughness usually falls, so an ultra-high-strength steel at 1500 MPa working stress with KIC of 50 tolerates only about 0.35 millimetres — smaller than many weld defects and below the reliable detection threshold of routine inspection. This is the leak-before-break principle in reverse, and it explains the deep engineering suspicion of very high strength steels in critical tension applications.

Temperature transforms behaviour. Body-centred cubic metals — ordinary carbon and low-alloy steels among them — undergo a ductile-to-brittle transition over a narrow temperature band, typically somewhere between minus 50 and plus 30 degrees Celsius depending on composition, grain size and thickness. Above it they absorb large energy and tear; below it they cleave with almost no plastic work. The Charpy V-notch impact test measures this, and a transition temperature is specified in codes for exactly this reason. The Liberty ships of the Second World War made the lesson unforgettable: roughly 1500 hulls suffered brittle fractures and about a dozen broke completely in two, the failures concentrated in cold North Atlantic water, initiating at square hatch corners in welded plate whose steel had a transition temperature above the sea temperature. The Titanic's plate has been argued to have been similarly notch-brittle at freezing water temperatures, though the extent of that contribution remains genuinely debated among metallurgists. Face-centred cubic metals — austenitic stainless steels, aluminium, copper, nickel — have no such transition and stay ductile to cryogenic temperatures, which is why liquefied gas tanks are built from 9 percent nickel steel, stainless or aluminium rather than ordinary carbon steel.

sections.heading: Failure modes, diagnosis and what to do when it goes wrong
sections.body:
Structures announce distress in readable ways, and learning to read them converts a vague unease into a decision. Excessive deflection that recovers when the load leaves is an elastic stiffness problem and, while alarming, is not immediately a strength issue. Permanent sag that remains after unloading means the member has yielded, and its reserve has been spent. Flaking paint or mill scale on a steel tension face, or peeling rust in a line across a member, marks where the surface has strained plastically. Cracks in plaster or masonry running diagonally from window corners usually indicate differential movement or shear. In timber, a crushed area at a bearing point where fibres have compressed across the grain indicates bearing failure, and a longitudinal split from a bolt hole means the fastener spacing was too close to the end.

Diagnosis by fracture surface is a powerful skill. A flat, granular, bright fracture perpendicular to the tensile stress with little deformation means brittle cleavage, and the questions are temperature, material grade and a stress raiser. A necked, fibrous cup-and-cone surface with visible deformation means simple ductile overload, and the question is what applied more load than expected. A smooth region with concentric arrest marks progressing from a surface origin, ending in a rough final zone, means fatigue, and the origin points to the geometry that caused it. A rough surface with branching intergranular cracks and no deformation, in a stainless steel exposed to chlorides or a brass exposed to ammonia, suggests stress corrosion cracking, which needs a tensile stress, a susceptible alloy and a specific environment acting together and can occur at a small fraction of yield.

The immediate response to a suspect structure is unglamorous and effective. Remove the load, or reduce it as far as possible. Prop the member with a temporary support that itself has a clear path to solid ground — a prop on a floor that is itself failing achieves nothing. Keep people out from underneath and to the side, because a buckling member moves sideways and a snapped tension element whips. Do not attempt to bend a permanently deformed steel member back cold: it exhausts remaining ductility and can precipitate brittle fracture. Do not weld a repair onto a member under load without releasing the load first, because heating locally destroys strength exactly where the arc runs.

Longer-term repair follows from the mode. Overload calls for a bigger section, a shorter span or an added support. Buckling calls for restraint, which is often astonishingly cheap — a single bracing member at midspan can double a column's capacity. Fatigue calls for eliminating the stress raiser and, if a crack exists, drilling a stop hole at its tip as a temporary measure before proper repair. Brittle fracture calls for a tougher material or a warmer service environment. And in every case the underlying question is the same one Galileo asked: is the material where the force needs it to be, and is there enough of it there.

guides.title: Structural analysis: trusses, beams and frames
guides.summary: How engineers work out the forces inside structures: loads, supports and reactions, equilibrium, truss analysis by the method of joints and sections, shear and bending moment diagrams for beams, bending stress and deflection, frames, indeterminate structures, and buckling.

sections.heading: What Structural Analysis Does: From Loads to Internal Forces
sections.body:
Structural analysis is the discipline that answers a deceptively simple question: when loads are applied to a structure, what forces develop inside each of its parts, and how much does it move? Every bridge, roof, tower, floor and crane must carry its loads down to the ground through a chain of members, connections and supports, and the analyst's job is to trace that chain quantitatively, so that each link can then be sized, in steel, concrete, timber or aluminum, with a margin against failure. Analysis is thus the middle act of structural engineering: it sits between the loading codes that say what the structure must resist, and the design codes that say how strong a given member is. Get the analysis wrong and the most careful material design is built on fiction.

The method rests on three pillars that recur throughout this guide. The first is equilibrium: a structure at rest is not accelerating, so by Newton's laws the forces and moments on it, and on every piece cut from it, must sum to zero. The second is compatibility: the pieces of a structure remain connected as it deforms, so their movements must fit together. The third is the material law, most often Hooke's law of linear elasticity, in which deformation is proportional to force. For a large and useful class of structures, called statically determinate, equilibrium alone answers everything, which is why so much of this guide can be worked with no more than algebra and a free-body diagram. For the rest, the statically indeterminate structures, all three pillars must be used together, and a later section shows how.

Analysis always operates on an idealization, not on the structure itself. A real welded roof truss becomes a diagram of weightless line members joined by frictionless pins; a floor slab becomes a uniform load per meter on a line beam; a column base cast into concrete becomes a symbol meaning fixed. The art lies in choosing idealizations whose errors are small and conservative, and generations of comparison between calculation, laboratory testing and built performance have established which simplifications are safe. Modeling judgment, knowing that a connection assumed pinned will really transmit some moment, and whether that matters, distinguishes an analyst from a calculator.

The subject has a datable history worth a paragraph, because its ideas were hard-won. Galileo opened it in 1638 with his Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences, analyzing, imperfectly, the strength of a cantilever beam. Hooke stated his law of elasticity in 1678; Euler derived column buckling in 1744; Coulomb corrected the theory of bending in 1773, and Navier assembled modern beam theory in his 1826 lectures in Paris. The railway age forced the analysis of trusses in the 1840s, the twentieth century added systematic methods for indeterminate frames, and since the 1960s the finite element method, running on computers, has extended analysis to shapes no hand method could touch. Yet every finite element model is checked, and every engineer is trained, with the hand methods in this guide, because they expose the load paths and orders of magnitude that a screen of colored stress plots can hide. The sections that follow build the toolkit in the classical order: loads, supports, equilibrium, then trusses, beams and frames, and finally the complications, indeterminacy and buckling, that make real structures interesting.

sections.heading: Loads on Structures: Dead, Live, Snow, Wind and Earthquake
sections.body:
Before any force inside a structure can be computed, the forces applied to it must be established, and structural engineering divides them into families with different origins, magnitudes and degrees of uncertainty. Dead load is the permanent weight of the structure and everything fixed to it: the beams and columns themselves, floor slabs, roofing, cladding, pipework, fixed equipment. It is the best-known load, calculable from drawings and material densities, reinforced concrete at about 24 kilonewtons per cubic meter, steel at 77, softwood timber near 5, and it never goes away, which makes it both reliable and relentless; in long-span bridges the structure's own weight dominates everything else.

Live loads are the movable and the moving: people, furniture, stored goods, vehicles. Because they vary, codes prescribe statistical envelope values, and the numbers are worth knowing. American practice under the standard ASCE 7 uses 40 pounds per square foot, about 1.9 kilopascals, for dwellings, 50 psf, 2.4 kilopascals, for offices, 100 psf, 4.8 kilopascals, for assembly areas and corridors where crowds can pack; European practice under Eurocode 1 gives closely similar figures. Bridge live loads have their own notational vehicles, such as the HL-93 truck-and-lane model of American highway design. Snow load depends on climate and roof shape, from under 0.5 kilopascals in mild regions to several kilopascals in mountain country, with drifting against parapets and steps multiplying the local value; roofs collapse most often not under the code snow but under the drift the designer forgot.

Wind and earthquake are the lateral loads, and they size the skeletons of tall and long structures. Wind pressure grows with the square of speed, roughly 0.6 kilopascals at a 100 kilometer per hour gust and rising steeply beyond, modified by height, terrain, and the aerodynamics of the building's shape, with suction on leeward faces and roof edges often governing cladding. Earthquake loading is inertial: the ground accelerates and the structure's own mass generates the force, so seismic demand scales with weight and with the stiffness and ductility of the system, and modern codes convert a mapped ground motion into equivalent lateral forces or require dynamic analysis outright. To these are added, as projects demand, fluid and earth pressures, thermal expansion and contraction, settlement of supports, impact and vibration from machinery, and construction-stage loads that can exceed anything in service.

Because loads are uncertain and rarely peak together, codes combine them with factors in defined combinations, the limit state method used worldwide since the late twentieth century. American strength design, for example, checks members against combinations such as 1.2 times dead plus 1.6 times live, and 1.2 dead plus wind plus 0.5 live, while serviceability, deflection and vibration under everyday conditions, is checked with unfactored loads. The analyst's obligation is to run every credible combination, including the counterintuitive ones: minimum gravity with maximum wind uplift has torn off roofs that the full-gravity case said were safe, and pattern loading, live load on some spans and not others, governs continuous beams. Load estimation is the least glamorous stage of analysis and the most consequential, since no elegance downstream can rescue a structure analyzed for the wrong demands.

sections.heading: Supports and Reactions: Pins, Rollers and Fixed Ends
sections.body:
A structure carries its loads to the ground through supports, and the way each support restrains the structure determines both the forces it can supply, called reactions, and the entire character of the analysis. Classical plane analysis recognizes three idealized support types, each a shorthand for what movement is prevented. A roller prevents translation in one direction only, supplying a single reaction force perpendicular to the surface it rolls on; the symbol is a triangle on circles, and the physical realizations include actual steel rollers and elastomeric bearing pads under bridge girders, and any connection intended to let the structure slide or expand. A pin, or hinge, prevents translation in both directions but allows rotation, supplying two reaction components, horizontal and vertical, but no moment; bolted clevis connections and bridge bearing pins realize it closely. A fixed support prevents translation and rotation alike, supplying two force components and a moment, three reactions in all; a column base with a heavy welded and anchored base plate, or a beam cast monolithically into a concrete wall, approaches fixity. To these, three-dimensional analysis adds their spatial generalizations, and practice adds the elastic support, a spring representing, for example, soil that yields under a footing.

Why the count of reactions matters so much becomes clear in the next sections: a plane structure has three equations of overall equilibrium, so three unknown reactions can be found from statics alone, while four or more demand the extra apparatus of indeterminate analysis. This is why the standard simply supported beam rests on one pin and one roller, three reactions, and not on two pins, four reactions: the roller is not carelessness but a deliberate release, and on bridges it is also the expansion joint, letting a deck lengthen in summer without straining the piers. Thermal movement is no triviality; a 100 meter steel deck warming by 30 degrees Celsius lengthens by about 36 millimeters, and a structure denied its roller must generate enormous internal forces to suppress that movement.

The supports having been identified, analysis begins with the free-body diagram, the single most important tool in this guide and arguably in all of mechanics. The structure is drawn isolated from the world; every support is replaced by the unknown reaction components it can exert, every load is drawn where it acts, and dimensions are marked. The discipline sounds trivial and is not: a large fraction of analysis errors, in classrooms and in practice, are free-body errors, a forgotten reaction component, a load applied twice, a moment omitted at a fixed end. The diagram externalizes the bookkeeping so the equations that follow are merely arithmetic.

A worked example fixes the pattern. A beam 6 meters long rests on a pin at the left end A and a roller at the right end B, carrying a 12 kilonewton point load 2 meters from A. Taking moments about A: 12 times 2 equals the vertical reaction at B times 6, so B carries 4 kilonewtons. Vertical equilibrium gives A's vertical reaction as 12 minus 4, which is 8 kilonewtons; with no horizontal loads, A's horizontal reaction is zero. The load divides in inverse proportion to its distance from each support, closer support carrying more, and this lever intuition, verified in three lines, is the seed from which every larger analysis in this guide grows. Real supports, finally, are never perfectly ideal, since pins have friction and fixed bases rotate slightly, and the analyst's protection is to know which way each idealization errs and to choose the assumption that is conservative for the quantity being checked.

sections.heading: Equilibrium: The Three Equations That Govern Every Plane Structure
sections.body:
All of classical structural analysis rests on one physical statement: a structure at rest stays at rest, so the resultant force and the resultant moment on it, and on any part of it, are zero. In a plane this yields exactly three independent scalar equations, the sum of horizontal forces equals zero, the sum of vertical forces equals zero, and the sum of moments about any point equals zero. In three dimensions there are six, three forces and three moments, but the plane trio carries most of design practice, because buildings and bridges are largely analyzed as assemblies of plane systems. The power of the principle lies in a fact easy to state and endlessly exploited: it applies to any free body whatsoever. The whole structure, a single member, a joint, or an arbitrary piece created by an imaginary cut, each must be in equilibrium, and every method in this guide, joints, sections, shear and moment diagrams, is nothing but a strategic choice of what to cut free.

Using the equations well is a small craft. A moment is a force times its perpendicular distance from the point about which moments are taken, and the freedom to choose that point is the analyst's chief tactical weapon: taking moments about a support eliminates the reactions passing through it, and taking moments about the intersection of two unknown forces eliminates both at once, yielding an equation with a single unknown. Sign conventions, counterclockwise moments positive, upward and rightward forces positive, are arbitrary but must be held consistently through a calculation; a negative answer is not an error but information, meaning the force acts opposite to the direction assumed, and the seasoned habit is to accept the algebra rather than flip arrows mid-solution. Distributed loads, expressed in kilonewtons per meter, are handled in equilibrium by their resultant: a uniform load of intensity w over length L acts, for external equilibrium purposes, as a single force wL at the midpoint, and a triangular distribution as its area acting through its centroid, one third of the way from the heavy end.

A worked example shows the machinery on something less symmetric than the last section's beam. A horizontal beam ABC is pinned at A, supported on a roller at B 4 meters away, and cantilevers 2 meters beyond to C, where it carries 10 kilonewtons downward; a uniform load of 6 kilonewtons per meter covers the 4 meter span AB. Replace the distributed load by its resultant, 24 kilonewtons at 2 meters from A. Moments about A: 24 times 2 plus 10 times 6 equals the reaction at B times 4, so B equals 27 kilonewtons. Vertical equilibrium: reaction at A equals 24 plus 10 minus 27, which is 7 kilonewtons. Two lines of algebra have delivered what intuition could not have guessed, that the roller carries nearly four times the pin's share, because the cantilevered load levers against it.

The three equations also define the boundary of their own usefulness. They are three; if a free body carries more than three unknowns, statics alone cannot finish the job, and if the structure's geometry allows motion without deformation, no set of reactions satisfies equilibrium under general load at all. Those two conditions, too many unknowns and hidden mechanisms, are the subject of the next section, and diagnosing them before solving is what separates methodical analysis from algebra performed hopefully.

sections.heading: Determinacy and Stability: Counting Unknowns Before Solving
sections.body:
Before solving any structure, an analyst counts. The three equilibrium equations of plane statics can determine at most three unknowns per independent free body, so comparing the number of unknown forces with the number of available equations tells you, before any algebra, which of three situations you face. If the counts match and the geometry is sound, the structure is statically determinate: statics alone yields every reaction and internal force, and the methods of the following sections finish the job. If unknowns exceed equations, the structure is statically indeterminate, or redundant; it is not unsolvable, but it withholds its forces until member stiffness and deformation are brought into the analysis, by the methods described near the end of this guide. The excess count is called the degree of indeterminacy. If equations exceed unknowns, the structure is a mechanism: it can move without deforming, cannot carry general load, and no solution exists, which is nature's way of rejecting the design outright.

For trusses the count has a famous compact form. With m members, r reaction components and j joints, each joint supplies two equilibrium equations, force balance in two directions, while the unknowns are the m member forces and the r reactions. Determinacy therefore requires m plus r to equal 2j. A simply supported triangle, three members, three reactions, three joints, gives 3 plus 3 equals 6, exactly 2 times 3: determinate. Add a diagonal to a braced quadrilateral so that both diagonals are present and the count comes out one high: indeterminate to the first degree, one member more than statics can apportion. Remove a diagonal from a rectangle of four members and the count comes out low: a mechanism, and the rectangle obligingly lozenges sideways. For beams and frames the equivalent count compares reactions plus three internal unknowns per member against three equations per rigid piece plus one per internal hinge, and tabulated formulas exist, but the principle is identical.

The counting rule, however, is necessary and not sufficient, and the fine print has collapsed structures. The count can be satisfied globally while the members are arranged badly, one panel doubly braced and its neighbor unbraced, so that part of the structure is redundant and part is a mechanism, summing deceitfully to the right total. Geometry can also betray a correct count: three reaction components whose lines of action all pass through one point, or are all parallel, cannot resist a moment about that point or a force along that direction, a condition called geometric or critical instability. The reliable habit is therefore to count and to inspect: trace how each part is braced, check that reactions are neither concurrent nor parallel, and imagine pushing the structure in each direction and rotation, asking what resists.

Determinacy is also a design decision with consequences beyond solvability. Determinate structures are insensitive to support settlement and temperature change, since a settling support merely moves a determinate beam without straining it, and their forces are predictable regardless of member stiffness, which is why many long bridges are deliberately articulated with hinges. Indeterminate structures are stiffer, distribute load among multiple paths, and can survive the loss of a member by rerouting force, the property called redundancy that saves lives in fires, collisions and blast, but they charge for these virtues by developing stresses under settlement and temperature that a determinate cousin would shrug off. Counting, then, is not bookkeeping; it is the first reading of a structure's character.

sections.heading: Trusses: How Triangles Turn Loads into Pure Push and Pull
sections.body:
A truss is a structure that refuses to bend by refusing to be anything but triangles. It is assembled from straight members connected at their ends into triangulated frameworks, and its defining trick is geometric: a triangle is the only polygon whose shape is fixed by the lengths of its sides. A rectangle of four pinned bars can lozenge sideways without any bar changing length; add one diagonal and the shape is locked, deformable only by actually stretching or shortening a member. Triangulation thus converts every applied load into axial forces, pure tension or pure compression along each member, and axial force is the cheapest way to carry load that structural engineering knows: a slender steel rod can carry in tension a force that would require a deep, heavy beam to carry in bending. That economy is why trusses appear wherever spans are long and weight is precious, in roofs, bridges, cranes, transmission towers, scaffolding and spacecraft.

The classical analysis rests on three idealizations. Members are connected by frictionless pins; loads are applied only at the joints; member weight is negligible or assigned to the joints. Under these assumptions each member is a two-force body, loaded only at its two ends, and equilibrium of a two-force body requires the forces to be equal, opposite and collinear, that is, directed along the member. Every member force is then a single number, positive in tension, pulling on its joints, or negative in compression, pushing on them, and the entire truss is solved when those numbers are known. Real trusses have gusset plates or welds rather than pins, and the bending these rigid joints introduce, called secondary stresses, is real but typically small in well-proportioned trusses with slender members, which is why the pin idealization survived from the nineteenth century into modern practice, now routinely checked by computer.

The standard forms carry the names of their nineteenth-century patentees, and reading them is part of structural literacy. The railway boom of the 1840s made truss design a competitive industry: Thomas and Caleb Pratt patented in 1844 the form with vertical posts and diagonals sloping down toward midspan, which under gravity load puts the long diagonals in tension and the short verticals in compression, an ideal division of labor for iron and steel, and the Pratt and its descendants became the default American bridge truss. William Howe's 1840 truss reverses the diagonals, suiting timber compression members. James Warren's 1848 form uses alternating equilateral diagonals with no verticals, elegant and economical, and is the shape of most modern highway girder-truss spans and space frames. The K-truss subdivides panels to shorten compression members; the Baltimore and Pennsylvania trusses do likewise for long spans. At the heroic end of the scale stand the Forth Railway Bridge of 1890, its 520 meter cantilever spans built from steel tubes, and the Quebec Bridge, whose 1907 collapse during construction, killing 75 workers, remains the discipline's sharpest lesson on compression members and appears again in the buckling section.

Reading a truss qualitatively is a skill worth acquiring before any calculation: under gravity load, the top chord of a simply supported truss is in compression and the bottom chord in tension, mirroring the flanges of a beam, while the web members shuttle shear between them, alternating sense according to the diagonals' slope. The next two sections make this reading quantitative, and a well-trained eye checking a computer output against it is the everyday form of quality control.

sections.heading: The Method of Joints: Solving a Truss Node by Node
sections.body:
The method of joints is the systematic way to find every member force in a determinate truss, and it is nothing more than the equilibrium principle applied at the smallest possible scale. Each joint of a truss, isolated as a free body, is a point acted on by the applied loads at that joint, any support reactions there, and the axial forces of the members meeting there, each directed along its member. A point has no size, so moments vanish identically, and only the two force equations remain: the sum of horizontal components equals zero, and the sum of vertical components equals zero. Two equations solve two unknowns, so the whole art of the method is order of march: begin at a joint where no more than two member forces are unknown, solve it, and let each solved member feed its now-known force to the joint at its other end, opening the next joint in turn. In a simply supported truss the natural entry points are the support joints, reached after the reactions have been found from equilibrium of the whole truss.

Conventions keep the bookkeeping honest. Assume every unknown member tensile, drawing its force arrow pulling away from the joint; then a positive result confirms tension and a negative result announces compression, with no re-drawing and no lost signs. Resolve each inclined member's force by its geometry, using the member's length proportions directly, a force F in a member with horizontal projection 3 and vertical projection 4 on a length of 5 contributes 3F over 5 horizontally and 4F over 5 vertically, which avoids trigonometric round-off and error. Work joint by joint, and use the final joint, where every member is already known, as a built-in check: its two equations must balance identically, and if they do not, an error lies upstream.

A worked example makes the march concrete. Take a Warren truss of two equilateral panels, span 8 meters, height about 3.46 meters: bottom chord joints A, C, E, top chord joints B and D, members AB, BC, CD, DE forming the zigzag, bottom chords AC and CE, top chord BD, with a pin at A, a roller at E, and 20 kilonewtons downward at C. Symmetry gives each reaction 10 kilonewtons upward. At joint A, two unknowns meet: AB at 60 degrees and AC horizontal. Vertical equilibrium: the vertical component of AB balances the 10 kilonewton reaction, so AB times sine 60 equals 10, giving AB equal to 11.55 kilonewtons, and the sign convention shows it compressive, pushing down the slope into the joint. Horizontal equilibrium: AC equals the horizontal component of AB, 11.55 times cosine 60, which is 5.77 kilonewtons tension. Joint B now has two unknowns, BC and BD; its equations give BC as 11.55 kilonewtons tension and BD as 11.55 kilonewtons compression, and symmetry finishes the right half. The pattern predicted qualitatively in the previous section has become numbers: compressed top chord, tensioned bottom chord, diagonals alternating.

The method generalizes without modification to any size of determinate truss and is the algorithm inside computer truss solvers, which simply assemble all joint equations and solve them simultaneously rather than sequentially. Its one weakness is wholesale character: to know one member deep inside a large truss you must solve your way across the structure to reach it. The remedy, cutting straight to the member of interest, is the method of sections, next.
steps: Idealize the truss: confirm pin joints, joint loading and member layout, and verify determinacy by checking that members plus reactions equal twice the joints.
Find the support reactions by applying the three equilibrium equations to the whole truss as a single free body.
Select a starting joint where at most two member forces are unknown, typically at a support or a loaded end joint.
Draw the free body of that joint, showing applied loads, reactions and every member force as an arrow pulling away from the joint, the tension assumption.
Resolve each inclined member force into components using the member's geometry, and write the two equations of force equilibrium for the joint.
Solve the two equations; record each result with its sign, positive meaning tension and negative meaning compression.
Transfer each solved member force to the joint at the member's far end and move to the next joint that now has no more than two unknowns.
Repeat around the truss until all members are solved, exploiting symmetry of geometry and loading to halve the work where it exists.
Use the final joint, where all members are known, as a check: both equilibrium equations must balance within rounding, or an upstream error exists.
Summarize the results in a force table or annotated diagram, marking tension and compression, ready for member design.

sections.heading: The Method of Sections and Zero-Force Members
sections.body:
When only a few member forces are wanted, or when a specific member deep in a large truss must be checked, marching joint by joint from a support is wasteful, and the method of sections goes straight to the target. The idea extends the free-body principle from a point to a region: slice the truss in imagination with a cut that passes through the member of interest and at most two others, choose either side of the cut as a free body, and apply all three equilibrium equations, two forces and one moment, to that piece. The cut member forces appear as external forces on the piece, directed along their members, tension assumed as before, and three equations solve the three of them at once. The tactical heart of the method is the moment equation and the freedom to place its center anywhere: taking moments about the point where two of the three cut members intersect eliminates both from the equation and delivers the third in a single line. For parallel-chord trusses, where chords never intersect, the complementary tactic is the shear form: the vertical equilibrium of the cut piece is resisted only by the diagonal, so the diagonal's vertical component equals the shear carried across the panel.

A worked example shows the directness. Take a Pratt truss of six 3 meter panels, span 18 meters, height 3 meters, simply supported, with 15 kilonewtons at each of the five interior bottom joints; each reaction is then 37.5 kilonewtons. To find the top chord force in the third panel, cut vertically through that panel, severing the top chord, the diagonal and the bottom chord, and take the left piece. Moments about the bottom joint 6 meters from the support, where diagonal and bottom chord meet: the reaction contributes 37.5 times 6, the first two panel loads contribute 15 times 3 and 15 times 0 as placed, and the top chord force times the 3 meter height must balance: 225 minus 45 gives 180, so the chord force is 60 kilonewtons, compression by its sense. One moment equation replaced the solution of five joints, and the same cut's vertical equation hands over the diagonal: vertical component equals 37.5 minus 30, so 7.5 kilonewtons, fixing the diagonal at 7.5 times the ratio of its length to its height.

The method also trains the structural eye through its byproduct, the spotting of zero-force members, members that carry nothing under a given load case. Two rules, both instant corollaries of joint equilibrium, find them by inspection. First, at an unloaded joint where exactly two non-collinear members meet, both are zero, since nothing exists to balance either one's transverse component. Second, at an unloaded joint where three members meet and two are collinear, the third is zero, and the collinear pair carry equal force through the joint. Applied repeatedly, these rules can strike a surprising fraction of a truss's members from a load case before any equation is written. The members are not useless, and this is the point students miss: they brace compression chords against buckling, halve unsupported lengths, and stand ready for other load cases, wind, unbalanced snow, a moving vehicle, under which they come alive. A member that is zero under full uniform load may be the one that matters under load on half the span.

Joints and sections together make a complete toolkit for determinate trusses: sections for the chords and critical diagonals of large structures, joints for full solutions and final checks, inspection rules to prune the work, and each method checking the other, which is precisely how hand verification of computer output proceeds in practice.

sections.heading: Beams: Shear Force and Bending Moment Diagrams
sections.body:
A beam is a member loaded transversely, across its axis, and unlike a truss member it cannot escape into pure push and pull: it carries load by bending. At every cross-section of a loaded beam, the material transmits two internal actions from one side to the other, a shear force V, the transverse force one side exerts on the other, and a bending moment M, the couple that accompanies it, and the whole craft of beam analysis is to map how V and M vary along the span. The maps are the shear force diagram and the bending moment diagram, and they are the most used drawings in structural engineering, because the peak moment sizes the beam and the peak shear checks its web and connections.
