The quantities are defined by the same free-body logic as everything else: cut the beam at a station x, take either piece, and V and M at that cut are whatever forces and couple restore its equilibrium. The usual sign convention takes positive shear as the pair tending to rotate the element clockwise, and positive moment as sagging, concave upward, tension on the bottom fiber, the shape of a smile.

Two differential relations, obtained by writing equilibrium of a thin slice of beam, organize the whole subject: the slope of the shear diagram equals the negative of the load intensity, and the slope of the moment diagram equals the shear. From them flow the working rules that let diagrams be sketched almost without calculation: over unloaded lengths the shear is constant and the moment varies linearly; under uniform load the shear varies linearly and the moment is a parabola; a point load steps the shear by its own value and kinks the moment; an applied couple steps the moment directly; and, most usefully of all, the moment reaches its extreme where the shear passes through zero, since the moment's slope vanishes there. The change in moment between any two stations equals the area under the shear diagram between them, which turns diagram construction into bookkeeping of areas.

The canonical cases deserve memory, because they calibrate every estimate an engineer ever makes. A simply supported beam of span L under a central point load P has reactions P over 2, a shear diagram stepping from plus P over 2 to minus P over 2 at midspan, and a triangular moment diagram peaking at PL over 4. The same beam under uniform load w per unit length has reactions wL over 2, a shear diagram sloping linearly from plus wL over 2 to minus wL over 2, crossing zero at midspan, and a parabolic moment diagram peaking at wL squared over 8, the most quoted formula in structural engineering. A cantilever of length L with a tip load P carries constant shear P and a moment growing linearly to PL at the fixed end; under uniform load its fixed-end moment is wL squared over 2. Numbers make them tangible: a 6 meter simply supported beam under 10 kilonewtons per meter carries a peak moment of 10 times 36 over 8, which is 45 kilonewton-meters, and peak shear of 30 kilonewtons at each support.

Continuous beams, resting on three or more supports, are statically indeterminate and wait for the methods near the end of this guide, but their qualitative diagrams are worth knowing now: interior supports develop hogging moments, tension on top, typically of magnitude comparable to the span moments they relieve, which is why continuous construction is efficient and why reinforcement in a concrete floor runs over the supports as well as under the spans. The diagrams, finally, are not an academic ritual: they are the beam's biography under load, and reading them fluently, knowing where the structure works hardest and why, is the core literacy this guide exists to teach.

sections.heading: Bending Stress and Section Shape: The Flexure Formula
sections.body:
The bending moment diagram says how hard each cross-section of a beam must work; the flexure formula says what that work costs the material. When a beam bends, its fibers on the convex side stretch and those on the concave side shorten, and somewhere between lies a surface that does neither, the neutral axis, which for a homogeneous elastic beam passes through the centroid of the cross-section. Strain therefore varies linearly across the depth, and with Hooke's law so does stress, from peak tension at one face through zero at the neutral axis to peak compression at the other. Summing the contributions of every fiber to the internal couple yields the formula assembled by Navier in 1826 from a century of partial results: the stress sigma at distance y from the neutral axis equals M times y divided by I, where M is the bending moment and I is the second moment of area of the cross-section, the integral of area times distance squared about the neutral axis. The extreme fiber stress, which governs design, is M times c over I, with c the distance to the farthest fiber, and the ratio I over c is packaged as the section modulus S, so that peak stress equals M over S: one number for the demand, one for the section, division for the verdict.

The second moment of area is the hero of the story, because distance enters it squared: material far from the neutral axis is disproportionately valuable, and material near it is nearly wasted. For a rectangle of width b and depth h, I equals b h cubed over 12, so doubling the depth of a beam multiplies its stiffness by eight and its strength by four, while doubling its width merely doubles both, which is why joists stand on edge and why a ruler that flops flatwise is stiff edgewise. Follow the logic to its conclusion and the material should flee the middle entirely, piling up at top and bottom, and that conclusion, drawn in wrought iron by the railway engineers of the 1840s, is the I-beam: two flanges doing the bending work, joined by a thin web whose job is the shear. The numbers justify the shape's dominance: a standard 310 millimeter deep steel universal beam of 40 kilograms per meter has a section modulus around 560 cubic centimeters, several times that of a solid square bar of equal weight. With steel yielding at 250 to 350 megapascals for common grades and an elastic modulus of 200 gigapascals, a designer checks that M over S, with load factors applied, stays below the design strength, and the same formula, with different constants, governs aluminum, timber and, with modification for cracking, reinforced concrete.

Shear has its own, quieter story. The transverse shear force V is carried by shear stresses distributed over the section, computed by the companion formula V Q over I b, peaking at the neutral axis, exactly where bending stress vanishes, so the two demands share the section rather than compounding; in an I-beam the web carries nearly all the shear at a nearly uniform stress, and the practical check is simply V divided by web area against the material's shear strength. Shear rarely governs long beams but rules short, heavily loaded ones, and it explains the classic failure of timber, which splits horizontally along the grain at the neutral axis, where longitudinal shear is greatest.

Two cautions complete the picture. The flexure formula is elastic and local: it says nothing about the section's tendency to buckle sideways or cripple, guarded against in the final section, and beyond first yield, steel sections carry further moment into the plastic range, the basis of plastic design, up to the plastic moment at which the whole section flows. But as a lens for reading structures, sigma equals M c over I is unmatched: it explains at a glance why bridges deepen over their piers, why a drilled hole matters more at a flange than at mid-depth, and why depth is the currency in which bending is paid.

sections.heading: Deflection and Serviceability: How Much Bending Is Too Much
sections.body:
A beam can be strong enough and still fail its occupants. Floors that bounce underfoot, partitions that crack over a sagging beam, doors that stick beneath one, machinery misaligned by supports that yield, none of these involve broken material, and all are failures of serviceability, the fitness of a structure for use. Analysis therefore computes not only stresses but movements, and design codes bound them: the traditional limit for beams supporting plastered ceilings and brittle finishes is a live-load deflection of span over 360, with span over 240 or 180 accepted for less sensitive conditions, so a 6 meter beam under a plastered ceiling is allowed about 17 millimeters. Footbridges and long floors add dynamic serviceability, keeping natural frequencies and accelerations outside the range that walking excites, a lesson relearned publicly when the London Millennium Bridge opened in June 2000 and synchronized pedestrian footfall drove lateral sway that closed it two days later until dampers were retrofitted.

The mechanics of deflection start where the flexure formula left off: bending curvature at each station equals M divided by EI, the moment over the flexural rigidity, the product of elastic modulus and second moment of area. Integrating curvature along the beam once gives slope, twice gives deflection, the double integration method, with support conditions fixing the constants. From it, or from energy methods, come the standard results every engineer carries: a simply supported span L under uniform load w deflects at midspan by 5 w L to the fourth over 384 EI; under a central point load P, by P L cubed over 48 EI; a cantilever under a tip load deflects by P L cubed over 3 EI, and under uniform load by w L to the fourth over 8 EI. The scalings are the real lesson: deflection grows with the cube or fourth power of span, so doubling a span multiplies its uniform-load sag sixteenfold unless EI grows to match, which is why long spans are deep, and why deflection rather than strength governs the design of most floors and of stiff materials used efficiently. A number anchors it: the 6 meter beam of the previous section, a 310 millimeter steel section with I about 8,500 centimeters to the fourth under 10 kilonewtons per meter, sags 5 times 10 times 1296 times ten-to-the-eighth over 384 times 200,000 times 8,500 in consistent units, about 10 millimeters, span over 600, comfortably serviceable.

For deflections at arbitrary points, and for the indeterminate methods of the next sections, engineers use the energy route: the unit load method, a specialization of virtual work descending from John Bernoulli's principle and systematized in the nineteenth century by Maxwell and the Italian engineer Alberto Castigliano, whose 1873 theorem gives deflection as the derivative of strain energy with respect to load. The unit load recipe is mechanical: to find the deflection at a point, apply an imaginary unit force there, compute the moment diagram m it would cause, and integrate M m over EI along the structure, a calculation of areas that handles any support condition without integration constants.

Two real-world corrections round out the elastic theory. Shear deformation, ignored above, adds meaningfully to the deflection of deep, short beams and of thin-webbed sections. And time enters through materials: timber creeps, and reinforced concrete both cracks, reducing its effective I, and creeps under sustained load, so that a concrete beam's ten-year deflection may be two to three times its initial elastic value, which codes handle with long-term multipliers. Camber, fabricating a beam with an upward bow equal to the expected dead-load sag, is the practical absolution, and its presence on the fabrication drawings is the visible sign that someone did the arithmetic of this section.

sections.heading: Frames: Rigid Joints and Combined Actions
sections.body:
A frame is what results when members are connected by joints that transmit moment, rigid joints, so that beams and columns behave not as an assembly of individuals but as a single bent continuous through its corners. The portal frame, two columns and a beam rigidly joined, is the atom of the type, multiplied into the single-story portals of warehouses and supermarkets and stacked into the multistory skeletons of office buildings, a lineage that began when William Le Baron Jenney's Home Insurance Building of 1885 in Chicago carried its walls on an iron frame and matured into the moment-resisting steel and concrete frames of every modern city. The rigid joint changes everything analytically. In a pin-jointed structure each member minds its own business; in a frame, a moment arriving at a joint is shared among all members meeting there, so bending a beam bends its columns, and loads applied to one story ripple through the others. Frame members consequently carry all three internal actions at once, axial force, shear and bending moment, and their diagrams are drawn member by member around the bent, with the joint equilibrium, moments at a joint summing to zero, stitching the pieces together.

Rigid joints buy two structural virtues. First, efficiency in gravity: a beam whose ends are restrained by columns behaves partway toward a fixed-ended beam, whose midspan moment under uniform load is wL squared over 24 rather than the simply supported wL squared over 8, the difference having migrated to the ends as hogging moments the columns help carry. Second, and historically decisive, lateral resistance: a frame resists wind and earthquake through the bending of its own members, no diagonal braces interrupting the architecture, the columns and girders racking against their joints. The price is that frames are almost always statically indeterminate, a single fixed-base portal is indeterminate to the third degree, and their internal forces depend on member stiffnesses, so analysis needs the methods of the next section or their computer descendants.

Hand analysis nonetheless penetrated frames long before computers, through approximate methods that remain the standard tools of estimation and checking. For gravity load, assuming inflection points, where moment passes through zero, at about a tenth of each beam span from its ends converts a continuous girder into a chain of determinate pieces. For lateral load, the portal method, published in the early twentieth century, assumes an inflection point at the midheight of every column and midspan of every girder, and distributes story shear among columns, interior columns classically taking twice the share of exterior ones; the cantilever method treats the whole bent as a vertical cantilever with column axial forces proportional to distance from the centroid, better for tall slender frames. These assumptions, checked against exact analysis, err by percentages acceptable for preliminary design, and their real value today is diagnostic: an engineer who can sketch the expected moment diagram of a wind-loaded frame, inflection points at midheights, moments peaking at the joints, can spot at a glance when a computer model has a support coded wrongly.

Frames also introduce behaviors trusses never show. Sway, the lateral drift of the frame under unsymmetric load or geometry, adds unknowns and couples stories together; drift limits, commonly height over 400 to 500 under wind, size many tall frames before strength does. Axial load in columns interacts with bending, the P-delta effect, a column displaced sideways carries its axial force at an eccentricity, generating extra moment, which analysis must include for slender frames and which foreshadows the buckling of the final section. And the joints themselves, the panel zones where beam flanges deliver their forces into column webs, are structural members in their own right, a fact underlined by the fractured welded connections found across Los Angeles after the Northridge earthquake of January 1994, which sent an entire profession back to the laboratory to requalify its standard moment connection. The frame is the workhorse of building structure, and its lesson is continuity: in a rigid skeleton, nothing bends alone.

sections.heading: Indeterminate Structures: Redundancy and How Engineers Solve Them
sections.body:
A statically indeterminate structure carries more supports or members than equilibrium can account for, and the extra unknowns are not a nuisance but a design choice: the continuous beam over many piers, the fixed-ended arch, the multistory frame, the doubly braced truss panel are all indeterminate, chosen for stiffness, economy and the ability to survive local damage by rerouting load. The price is analytical: since statics alone cannot apportion forces among redundant paths, the analyst must invoke the remaining pillars, compatibility of deformation and the stiffness of the members, and the history of structural engineering from 1860 to 1960 is largely the history of making that invocation tractable by hand.

Two dual strategies organize every method. The force method, also called the flexibility method, descending from James Clerk Maxwell's 1864 paper and Otto Mohr's development of it, treats redundant forces as the unknowns. Imagine removing redundants until the structure is determinate, the primary structure; compute how the primary structure deflects at the removed restraints under the real loads; then determine what redundant forces are required to push those deflections back to zero, a small system of compatibility equations whose coefficients are deflections per unit force, calculated by the unit load integrals of the deflection section. For a two-span continuous beam, one redundant, one equation, and the method delivers the interior support reaction in a page. The displacement method, its mirror, treats joint movements as the unknowns: write how member end forces depend on end rotations and translations, the stiffness relations, then demand equilibrium at every joint, and solve for the displacements. The slope-deflection equations, published in mature form by George Maney in 1915, are this method for frames by hand.

The method that actually carried the profession through the mid-century building boom was a scheme for solving the displacement equations without solving equations: moment distribution, published by Hardy Cross of the University of Illinois in a short 1930 paper in the Proceedings of the American Society of Civil Engineers. Lock every joint of the frame against rotation and compute the fixed-end moments each loaded span would then carry, wL squared over 12 at each end of a uniformly loaded fixed span, for instance. Then release the joints one at a time: an unbalanced joint moment is distributed among the members meeting there in proportion to their rotational stiffnesses, distribution factors, and half of each distributed moment travels to the member's far end, the carry-over factor of one half for uniform members. Iterating around the frame, the corrections shrink geometrically, and three or four passes yield moments within engineering accuracy. A generation of engineers analyzed hospitals, high-rises and bridges with nothing but this arithmetic, and the method survives in education because it makes stiffness and load-sharing physically visible: stiff members attract moment in exact proportion, which is the deepest single fact about indeterminate behavior.

The displacement method's systematic matrix form, assembling member stiffness relations into a global system solved by computer, arrived with the aerospace industry in the 1950s and became the direct stiffness method inside every modern analysis program, and its generalization to continua is the finite element method. What the computer did not change is the structure of engineering judgment the hand methods teach: indeterminate structures draw force toward stiffness, so a stiff path, a deep girder, a squat column, a wall, will carry more than its tributary share whether the designer intended it or not; support settlement and temperature, which determinate structures accommodate freely, induce real stresses in indeterminate ones, a differential settlement of centimeters can use up a continuous bridge's capacity; and redundancy is only as good as the ductility that lets force redistribute after a local failure. The I-35W Mississippi River bridge that collapsed in Minneapolis in August 2007, killing 13, was a determinate truss whose undersized gusset plates left no alternate path, and its lesson, that redundancy is a safety property worth paying the analytical price for, is written into modern bridge codes as explicit requirements for load path redundancy.

sections.heading: Buckling and Failure: Why Compression Is Treacherous
sections.body:
Everything to this point has assumed that a member fails when its material does, but compression members break the assumption spectacularly: a slender column can collapse sideways at a load that leaves its material stressed far below yield. The phenomenon is buckling, an instability rather than a strength failure, and it was solved in its ideal form by Leonhard Euler in 1744: a perfect pin-ended elastic column of length L and flexural rigidity EI carries at most the critical load P equal to pi squared EI over L squared, beyond which the straight form is unstable and the column bows. Every term teaches. The load capacity falls with the square of length, so doubling a strut's length quarters its buckling load; it rises with I, so material spread away from the axis, the tube, the wide flange, resists buckling exactly as it resists bending, which is why bicycle frames and scaffold standards are tubes; and the material's strength appears nowhere at all, only its stiffness E, so high-strength steel buys nothing against elastic buckling, one of design's recurring surprises. End conditions enter through an effective length: fixing both ends halves the effective length and quadruples the capacity, a cantilevered flagpole doubles it and quarters the capacity, and codes tabulate the factors.

Real columns are neither perfectly straight nor perfectly elastic, and the practical curve of strength against slenderness, the ratio of effective length to the section's radius of gyration, has three regions: short, stocky members that squash at the material's yield strength; long, slender members that follow Euler; and the treacherous middle, where initial crookedness, accidental eccentricity and locked-in residual stresses from rolling and welding interact, dragging real strength well below both ideal curves. Design rules, fitted to thousands of column tests, span the middle empirically. The intermediate regime is where the discipline learned its costliest lessons. The Quebec Bridge, in 1907 the longest cantilever ever attempted, collapsed during erection when the latticed compression chords, their true behavior falling in exactly this gap between theory and test, buckled under the structure's own growing weight, killing 75 workers; the inquiry remade compression member design, and the disaster stands behind the profession's rituals of independent checking. Buckling also operates at every scale within members: the thin compression flange of a beam can buckle locally, wrinkling like foil; a deep slender web can buckle in shear; and a whole beam bent about its strong axis can fail by lateral-torsional buckling, the compression flange escaping sideways while the tension flange anchors, which is why long beams are braced at intervals and why a plank on edge twists as it fails.

Buckling completes the catalogue of failure modes an analyst must imagine, alongside yielding in tension, fracture, especially brittle fracture at welds and cold temperatures, shear, connection failure, the I-35W gusset plates of the previous section, fatigue under repeated load, and the aeroelastic instabilities of flexible structures, made famous when the Tacoma Narrows suspension bridge tore itself apart in a 68 kilometer per hour wind in November 1940, filmed as its deck twisted in torsional flutter, a dynamic instability rather than simple resonance, and a permanent argument for testing shapes against the wind. Modern design addresses the whole catalogue through the limit state framework, factored loads against reduced resistances calibrated to target reliabilities, and through capacity design, deliberately making ductile modes weaker than brittle ones so that overload announces itself in stretching steel rather than snapping welds. The unifying habit of mind, and a fitting close to this guide, is the load path: follow every force from where it arises, through members, joints and supports, into the ground, asking at each station how it is carried, how the element could fail, and what would carry the force if it did. Structural analysis provides the numbers along that path; the questions are the engineering.
